# AI Research Lab

A reusable workspace for academic literature research. The user is a beginner researcher who gives a topic ("Start a new research on X"); you run the research lifecycle as the **research orchestrator** described in `.claude/agents/research-orchestrator.md` (delegation table and state ownership live there).

## Rules (full version: `docs/research-standards.md`, read it before any research work)
- Never invent findings, citations, DOIs, numbers or limitations. Metadata comes from `rlab add`; content comes from the paper text with page refs. Unknown → say "not reported" / "not found".
- Label every claim: **[V]** verified in the paper's data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Cite `[@key, p. N]`.
- Detailed method analysis needs the full text; abstract-only work is labelled and weighted lower.
- Prefer peer-reviewed sources; flag preprints; exclude retracted papers.
- Legal open access only. Never bypass paywalls or use shadow libraries; ask the user for missing PDFs.
- Never overwrite or delete `paper.pdf`, `fulltext.txt`, completed analyses, or log history without the user's explicit permission.
- A research gap is claimed only after a recorded novelty check.

## Tools
- `rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py` (run from this directory; `-h` lists commands). Use it for every deterministic step: project creation, search, adding papers (resolves + verifies metadata, rejects duplicates), PDF fetch/attach + text extraction, validation, BibTeX, citation checks, indexing, logging. Never hand-edit `metadata.json`, `registry.json`, `literature-matrix.*`, `references.bib` or `research/INDEX.md`.
- After changing project content, run `rlab index <id>`; log decisions with `rlab log <id> <phase> "<msg>"`.
- Skills (`.claude/skills/`): start-research, discover-papers, analyze-paper, compare-methods, find-gaps, write-literature-review, research-report, reading-guide, resume-research.
- Shareable Google Doc: `python3 scripts/md2gdoc.py --title T --subtitle S [--share anyone] [--pdf out.pdf] [--md out.md] a.md b.md ...` turns simple markdown (one file per page; see the script docstring) into a styled Google Doc owned by the user (auth via the google-doc-builder skill). Per-project reading guides live in `reports/reading-guide/` (`00-front.md`, `papers/<key>.md`, `99-back.md`, `order.txt`).
- External services in use: OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv, PubMed, doi.org, Europe PMC (no keys needed). Semantic Scholar is rate-limited without a key: use it via WebFetch only as a fallback. Unpaywall runs only if `RLAB_CONTACT_EMAIL` is set.

## Layout
- `research/registry.json` — all projects (via `rlab`); `research/INDEX.md` — human overview.
- `research/<id>/` — one project: `RESEARCH.md`, `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`, `STATUS.md`, `research-log.md`, `literature-matrix.md/.csv`, `evidence-matrix.md`, `gap-report.md`, `references.bib`, `search/`, `papers/<key>/{metadata.json,paper.pdf,fulltext.txt,analysis.md,paper.bib}`, `reports/`.
- `templates/` — project and analysis templates. `docs/` — standards. `tests/` — `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`.

## Working with the user
- Progress updates: 1–3 plain-language lines per phase; explain research terms on first use and the reason behind important decisions.
- Handle routine work yourself. Ask only for: scope/RQ choices that change direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, destructive actions.
- State lives in files, not in conversation memory: keep `STATUS.md` (Next actions, Blocked / needs user) current so any session can resume.
- [Reading guide doc preference](reading-guide-doc-preference.md) — end every project with plain-English reading guide as public-link Google Doc

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications that cut a real corner with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic) with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and upgrade path (`# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`).

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

# Research standards

The rules every skill and agent in this workspace follows. One source of truth: change rules here, not in individual skills.

## 1. Evidence labels
Every substantive statement about a paper or the literature carries one label:

| Label | Short | Meaning | Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| VERIFIED | [V] | Checked against the paper's own data, tables, figures or results text. | Page ref `(key, p. N)` |
| AUTHOR-CLAIM | [A] | The authors state it; we cannot independently check it (e.g. claims of novelty, interpretations, conclusions beyond the data). | Page ref |
| INTERPRETATION | [I] | Our own reasoning, synthesis or critique. | Say what it is based on |

Page refs use the `=== [PDF page N] ===` markers in `fulltext.txt` (PDF page index, not printed page number). When a quote is used, it is copied verbatim from `fulltext.txt`.

Citation syntax:
- Inside a paper's own `analysis.md`: `(p. N)`.
- Everywhere else (evidence matrix, reports, reviews): pandoc style `[@key, p. N]` or `[@key1; @key2]`. Keys are the folder names under `papers/`. This works with `references.bib` and pandoc.
- `rlab cite-check <project> <file...>` must pass before any written document is handed to the user.

## 2. Never invent
- Every DOI, title, author, year and venue comes from `metadata.json` (resolved by `rlab add` from Crossref/OpenAlex/arXiv/PubMed). Never type a DOI from memory.
- Every finding, number, limitation and quote comes from the paper text. If the paper does not report something, write "not reported".
- Every citation in written output uses an existing paper key in the project. A claim with no source is either removed or labelled [I].
- If something cannot be found or verified, say so plainly. An honest "unknown" beats a plausible guess.

## 3. Source quality tiers
Prefer higher tiers; state the tier when it matters to the argument.

1. Peer-reviewed journal articles and full papers at reputable conferences (`venue_kind: published`); systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top for evidence synthesis.
2. Peer-reviewed workshop papers, book chapters from academic publishers.
3. Preprints (`venue_kind: preprint`, e.g. arXiv): usable, always flagged "not peer-reviewed". If a published version exists, use it instead.
4. Theses, technical reports, grey literature: background only, flagged.
5. Blogs, news, Wikipedia, vendor material: never cited as evidence. May guide searching.

`venue_kind: published` means the work appeared in a journal or proceedings; it is not proof of rigorous review. Watch for predatory venues (unknown publisher, implausibly fast review, no indexing) and flag them.
Retracted papers (`RETRACTED` flag from `rlab`) are excluded from evidence; mention only as retracted.

## 4. Reading depth
- Detailed methodology, dataset, setup, metrics, findings and limitations require the full text (`evidence_basis: full-text`).
- Abstract-only analysis (`evidence_basis: abstract-only`) may fill objective and headline claims labelled [A] only. All method sections say "full text not available". Abstract-only papers carry less weight in synthesis and gap claims; say so.
- Read the whole paper: methods, results, tables, limitations, appendix if relevant. Note skipped parts in "Analyst notes".

## 5. Critical appraisal checklist
For every empirical paper check and record:
- Sample size and how it was chosen; power or uncertainty reporting.
- Baselines and whether they are fair and current.
- Evaluation design: train/test separation, leakage, cross-validation, held-out data, blinding, control groups.
- Statistical testing: tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals, multiple comparisons.
- Reproducibility: data, code, hyper-parameters, protocol available?
- Conflicts of interest and funding where relevant.
- Whether conclusions go beyond the data (mark those [A] and note it).

Evidence strength: **strong** = adequate N, sound design, replicated or consistent across studies; **moderate** = sound design but single study or limited N; **weak** = small/unclear N, design flaws, abstract-only, or preprint without replication.

## 6. Contradictions
When papers disagree: record both sides in the evidence matrix "Contradictions" section with page refs, then compare data, population, method, metric and time. Offer an explanation only as [I]. Never silently pick a side.

## 7. Research gaps and novelty
A gap is reported only when:
1. It is supported by evidence from analysed papers (explicit future-work statements, consistent limitations, contradictions, untested populations/conditions, missing method comparisons).
2. A dedicated novelty check was run: at least 3 targeted searches (`rlab search`) across at least 2 sources, recent years included, plus a web search for very recent work. Queries, date and closest hits are recorded in the gap entry.
3. Confidence is stated. "No paper found" is phrased as "we found no paper that ... (searches on DATE)", never "this has never been studied".

## 8. Copyright and access
- Download only legal open-access copies: OpenAlex/Unpaywall OA locations, arXiv, Europe PMC, publisher OA pages. `rlab fetch` enforces this and refuses shadow libraries.
- Never bypass paywalls, logins, CAPTCHAs, or rate limits. Never use Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive or similar.
- When no OA copy exists: tell the user and ask them to obtain it through their library, then `rlab attach`. Otherwise analyse abstract-only and label it.
- Quotes stay short and attributed. PDFs stay inside the project folder and are not redistributed.

## 9. Preservation
- Original PDFs (`paper.pdf`), extracted text (`fulltext.txt`) and completed analyses (`status: complete`) are never overwritten or deleted without the user's explicit permission. A hook asks the user first (once `setup/claude-settings.json` is installed).
- Analysis status flow: `draft` (in progress) -> `ready` (analyst self-check passed) -> `complete` (critical review passed). Fix review findings while the analysis is `ready`.
- Revisions to a completed analysis go in a new section `## Revision YYYY-MM-DD` with what changed and why, after the user agrees.
- `research-log.md` is append-only.

## 10. Talking to the user (a beginner researcher)
- Progress updates: short, what was done, what was found, what is next.
- Explain research terms on first use in one plain sentence (e.g. "a *systematic review* is a study that collects and evaluates all studies on a question").
- Explain important decisions and their reason: scope cuts, exclusions, weak evidence, gaps.
- Ask only for: scope or research-question choices that change the direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, and anything destructive.

name: reading-guide
description: Build a plain-language Reading Guide for a project (overview, one 1–2 page brief per paper, gaps and opportunities, glossary) and publish it as a styled, shareable Google Doc. Use at the end of every research run (after research-report), or when the user asks for paper summaries, documentation, a doc, or a shareable link.
---

# Reading guide + shareable Google Doc

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md). Audience: the user, a beginner who has NOT read the papers. Plain English, short sentences, every technical term explained on first use.

Input: project id. Needs complete analyses, `evidence-matrix.md`, `gap-report.md`, the research report. Output folder: `research/<id>/reports/reading-guide/`.

## 1. Write (delegate to `academic-writer`, in parallel)
- **Paper briefs** — 5–6 paper keys per agent, one file each: `reports/reading-guide/papers/<key>.md`. Source: `papers/<key>/analysis.md` (keep its corrections and labels), `metadata.json`, `fulltext.txt` for checks. ~600–1200 words, exactly this structure:
  - `## <Full paper title>`
  - `> **Takeaway:** <1–2 sentences>`
  - table `| Item | Detail |`: Authors · Year · Venue · Status (Peer-reviewed / Preprint; note if our copy is an arXiv version) · Identifier · Paper type · Relevance to us (High/Medium/Low — RQs)
  - `### In plain words` · `### How they did it` · `### Data and setup` · `### Key findings` (4–8 bullets, numbers, label + `[@key, p. N]`) · `### Limitations and weaknesses` · `### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open` (link gap IDs) · `### Why it matters for your research` · `### Connections to other papers`
- **Front/back matter** — one agent writes:
  - `00-front.md`: `# Overview` — topic + RQs in plain words, how to use the guide (labels, citations, preprints), main findings per RQ with evidence strength, paper map table (all papers, grouped), 5 papers to read first, where studies disagree.
  - `99-back.md`: `# Research Gaps and Opportunities` (each gap: callout, evidence, novelty verdict + closest prior work, contribution, beginner study design, feasibility, risks; any follow-up topic novelty checks in `reports/`; next-steps checklist; recommended papers not yet included), `# Glossary` (table, 30+ terms), `# About this guide` (method, dates, limitations).
  - `order.txt`: paper keys in paper-map order.
- Markdown the converter understands: `#`/`##`/`###`, paragraphs, `- ` bullets, `1. ` lists, pipe tables, single-paragraph `> ` callouts, `**bold**`. No nested bullets, italics, links, HTML, images, code.
- Every agent finishes with `rlab cite-check <id> <its files>` → OK.

## 2. Check
`rlab cite-check <id>` on all guide files; every key in `order.txt` has a brief.

## 3. Publish
Write `reports/reading-guide/10-papers.md` (`# Paper Summaries` + one line on how each brief is organised). Make appendix copies (the user wants the whole research outcome at the end): `appendix-a-research-report.md` (latest `reports/research-report-*.md`), `appendix-b-methodology-comparison.md`, `appendix-c-evidence-matrix.md` — each a copy with its first `# ` heading renamed to `# Appendix A: Full Research Report` etc. Then from the workspace root:

```bash
G=research/<id>/reports/reading-guide
python3 scripts/md2gdoc.py --title "Reading Guide: <short topic>" --subtitle "<full topic>" \
  --share anyone --md research/<id>/reports/reading-guide-YYYY-MM-DD.md --pdf research/<id>/reports/reading-guide-YYYY-MM-DD.pdf \
  $G/00-front.md $G/10-papers.md $(sed "s#^#$G/papers/#; s#\$#.md#" $G/order.txt) $G/99-back.md $G/appendix-*.md
```

Later additions go into the same doc: `python3 scripts/md2gdoc.py --append <DOC_ID> new.md`. Spot-check a few PDF pages (Read the PDF) before sending the link.

`--share anyone` = anyone with the link can view (the user's chosen default; use `--share none` if they ask for private). Auth comes from the google-doc-builder skill; on `invalid_grant` run its `gdoc_auth.py` and show the user the login URL. Rendering takes several minutes (Docs API write quota); run it in the background.

## 4. Record
Add the doc URL and file paths to `STATUS.md` (Next actions), `rlab log <id> writing "reading guide published: <url>"`. Tell the user the link, what is inside, and that local `.md`/`.pdf` copies are in `reports/`.

1:# Research questions — LLM-based vs Traditional Static Analysis and Deep Learning Approaches for Source Code Vulnerability Detection: A Comparative Review
5:## RQ1: How do LLM-based approaches compare with SAST tools and DL detectors in detection effectiveness (precision, recall, F1, false-positive rate) in head-to-head evaluations?
12:## RQ2: How do evaluation setups (benchmarks, languages, CWE coverage, synthetic vs. real-world code, data-leakage control) differ across studies, and how do they explain disagreements in reported results?
30:## RQ3: Do hybrid LLM + static-analysis approaches outperform either family alone, and what are the trade-offs in cost, speed and explainability?
37:## RQ4: Which vulnerability types (CWEs), languages and code scales does each family handle well or poorly?
44:## RQ5: What gaps and open problems remain for reliable, deployable LLM-based vulnerability detection?
1:# Research gap report — LLM-based vs Traditional Static Analysis and Deep Learning Approaches for Source Code Vulnerability Detection: A Comparative Review
10:## Novelty-check query log (2026-11-12)
62:## Positioning of our review
64:**Question.** Does a review or SLR already compare LLM-based, SAST and DL vulnerability detection through an evaluation-setup / benchmark-realism lens, i.e. arguing that benchmark design explains contradictory results?
66:**Verdict.** We found no review that does both of the following (searches on 2026-11-12: Q1–Q5, Q21, Q22, W1, W2):
72:**The four reviews in our corpus.**
83:**Closest reviews outside our corpus** (not analysed, abstract only, found via Q1–Q5, Q21, Q22, Q26, W1, W2):
95:**How our review should position itself** [I]:
104:**Risk.** With 24 papers (20 primary studies), the review must be framed as a *critical comparative review*, not a comprehensive SLR. Reviewers will likely point to qin2026review (the CAI 2026 review) and kaniewski2026systematic for the "evaluation pitfalls" message. The distinct contribution is the cross-family, contradiction-explaining angle, and the G1 re-analysis below would make it concrete.
108:## Ranked gaps (evidence strength × beginner feasibility)
121:## G1: Published results are not re-scored against trivial baselines or realistic prevalence; no shared evaluation protocol exists for comparing LLMs, SAST and DL
172:## G2: No same-benchmark, leakage-controlled comparison of LLMs vs semantic SAST vs fine-tuned DL on real, post-cutoff code with file or repository context
234:## G3: True-positive loss in LLM filtering of SAST alarms is not controlled per CWE on real security alerts
269:## G4: Hybrid LLM+SAST detectors lack independent replication that separates target, metric and labeller effects
300:## G5: Real-CVE LLM-vs-standard-SAST evidence is missing for PHP and Go (JavaScript and Python only partly covered)
348:## G6: No cost-per-confirmed-vulnerability comparison that includes human triage effort and a costed SAST and DL arm on the same targets
377:## Dropped or merged candidates
394:## Recommended for inclusion (not added; not analysed)

content.content:
## Ranked gaps (evidence strength × beginner feasibility)

| Rank | Gap | Evidence | Feasibility | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | No common evaluation protocol: published LLM/SAST/DL results are not *systematically, across studies* re-scored against trivial baselines and realistic prevalence (several single studies now do it for their own results) | strong (≥9 papers) | **easy** (re-analysis of published numbers) | medium–high (unchanged) |
| G2 | No same-benchmark, leakage-controlled LLM vs *semantic* SAST vs fine-tuned DL comparison on real, *post-cutoff* code *with file/repository context* (narrowed: a function-level, pre-cutoff C/C++ three-family comparison now exists) | strong (≥6 papers) | moderate | medium (narrowed) |
| G3 | True-positive loss in LLM filtering of SAST alarms is not controlled per CWE on real security alerts | moderate (2 papers + author future work) | easy–moderate | low–medium (unchanged) |
| G4 | Hybrid tools (IRIS, RepoAudit): no independent replication separating target, metric and labeller effects | moderate (contradictions C2, C6) | moderate–hard | medium (unchanged) |
| G5 | Real-CVE LLM-vs-*standard*-SAST evidence for PHP and Go (narrowed: LLM-only WordPress-plugin evidence and function-level Python/Java/JS three-family evidence now exist, abstract only) | moderate | moderate | low–medium (narrowed) |
| G6 | No cost-per-*confirmed*-vulnerability comparison that includes human triage effort and a costed SAST/DL arm on the same targets (narrowed: compute cost per TP for 8 LLMs now exists) | moderate | moderate (piggybacks on G2) | low–medium (narrowed) |

---

=== G1
8:    - khare: always-vulnerable rows appear among the best F1 values [@khare2025understanding, p. 16].
10:    - deininger (35.4% vulnerable sample): LLM F1 0.405–0.615 against always-vulnerable F1 0.523 [@deininger2026open, p. 7] [V]. At the natural 1:44 prevalence every LLM's precision is 2.3–3.8% against 2.21% for always-flag, with 25.6–41.9 false positives per true positive [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [V] (2.8–4.6% in the budget-matched second epoch [@deininger2026open, p. 17]).
17:    - gnieciak applies a lenient location rule only to LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6] [V].
18:    - The CASTLE prompt reveals the scoring scheme to the LLM [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9] [V].
20:  - **Headline LLM-vs-SAST numbers use five incompatible metrics**: macro F1, CASTLE score, accuracy, detection ratio, recall/SFDR [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 10; @khare2025understanding, p. 9; @zhou2024comparison, p. 5; @li2026llm, p. 11] [I].
24:  - **Statistics are rare.** Among the first 16 primary studies, only tan2026think applies significance tests to its main comparison [@tan2026think, p. 6] [I, our count]. Of the four second-pass papers, deininger2026open uses a paired bootstrap with Holm correction [@deininger2026open, p. 6] [V].
25:  - **The decision rule and the prompt can flip conclusions.** At the default argmax threshold the fine-tuned PrimeVul detector predicts all-safe despite ROC-AUC 0.845; the authors nearly reported this as "trained detectors are no better than LLMs" [@deininger2026open, p. 11] [V]. Prompt paraphrases change the winning LLM [@deininger2026open, p. 20] [V].
28:  - **In our corpus, within-study baselines only.** shu2026evaluating, deininger2026open and tashenova2026real report trivial baselines, and lu2025lab's chance level is derivable (see evidence above). PrimeVul's VD-S is also in the corpus. Each applies the baseline only to its own results; none re-scores other studies [I].
36:- **Second-pass verdict: unchanged (still open).** Trivial baselines are spreading as a *within-study* practice. This makes the gap's premise stronger: four further studies (deininger, tashenova, lu, and the abstract-only TSARKA study) show results at or near trivial levels. It does not fill the gap, because none of them re-scores other studies' published numbers on a common scale [I]. The contribution should now be framed as a *systematic cross-study* re-scoring, and it must credit these within-study baselines rather than claim to be the first to use them.
47:  - **Baselines:** always-vulnerable; random (P-C reference 22.70% for ding-style pairs); published dummy, word-count or token-count baselines where available. Use a study's own published baseline where it exists (shu, deininger, tashenova) and check that our formula reproduces it; this is a built-in validity check of the re-scoring.
=== G2
3:- **Second-pass verdict: narrowed.** deininger2026open fills the function-level, pre-cutoff, C/C++ version of this gap with lightweight SAST. What remains open: (a) post-cutoff targets, (b) file or repository context, (c) a semantic, build-based SAST arm such as CodeQL, and (d) a peer-reviewed non-C/C++ version (a function-level Python/Java/JS three-family preprint exists, abstract only; see novelty check).
6:    - khare2025understanding evaluates LLMs, SAST and DL, but CodeQL runs on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7] [V].
7:    - deininger2026open runs 8 zero-shot LLMs, Flawfinder 2.0.20, Cppcheck 2.21, Semgrep 1.175 and two CodeBERT detectors on the same 1549 PrimeVul C/C++ functions [@deininger2026open, p. 6; @deininger2026open, p. 10] [V]. Its limits are the ones that define what is left of G2:
8:      - CodeQL could not be run because the functions are unbuildable snippets [@deininger2026open, p. 10] [V];
9:      - all CVEs date from 2008–2022 and predate the models' training cutoffs, and recall is 7–15 points higher on pre-2020 CVEs [@deininger2026open, p. 24] [V];
10:      - function level, one dataset, C/C++ only [@deininger2026open, p. 25] [A];
11:      - the fine-tuned detector is in-distribution while the LLMs are zero-shot [@deininger2026open, p. 11] [A].
12:    - Its result shows why the gap still matters: the ranking depends on the metric. On balanced accuracy fine-tuned CodeBERT leads (0.765 vs ≤0.711 for LLMs); on precision at 1:44 prevalence Semgrep (26.0%, CI 5.7–66.9%) and strict Flawfinder (13.4%) lead, and every LLM is at 2.3–3.8% in the first epoch (2.8–4.6% budget-matched) [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 10; @deininger2026open, p. 17] [V].
13:  - **zhou2024comparison has no classic DL detector.** It compares fine-tuned and prompted LLMs with SAST [@zhou2024comparison, p. 4] [V].
20:    - LLM vs SAST rankings reverse between small programs, synthetic suites and repositories [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @khare2025understanding, p. 9; @li2026llm, p. 7] [V].
25:    - Only xiong2026sifting, li2026llm and lu2025lab test on post-cutoff or temporally separated code [@xiong2026sifting, p. 15; @li2026llm, p. 5; @lu2025lab, p. 4] [V]; none of the three runs all three families [I].
26:  - **Survey future work asks only for verified benchmarks.** The surveys' future directions call for verified, contamination-free, repository-level benchmarks [@zhou2025large, p. 22; @sheng2025llms, p. 25] [A], but not for a controlled three-family comparison [I]. deininger2026open plans a post-cutoff restriction [@deininger2026open, p. 24] [A].
=== G3
=== G4
6:    - Independent (li2026llm): 0 of 110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities and 92.77% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11] [V]; cost up to $1,247.66 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16] [V].
9:    - Independent: 97.80% vs 77.00% SFDR on new Java projects [@li2026llm, p. 12] [V].
10:  - **The independent study labels with an LLM it also evaluates.** li2026llm labels warnings with Codex, which it also evaluates [@li2026llm, p. 11] [V], so its labeller is not independent [I].
14:  - li2026llm (in corpus) is itself the only independent re-evaluation.
=== G5
14:    - li2026llm: broader languages and CWE classes [@li2026llm, p. 18] [A];
15:    - deininger2026open: other languages [@deininger2026open, p. 25] [A];
19:    - zhou2024comparison covers Python with roughly 8–10 test CVEs per language [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6] [I].
22:  - **Neef et al. 2026**, *Evaluating LLMs for Real-World Web Vulnerability Detection* (arXiv 2606.21397, v1 19 June 2026; to appear at the AI&CCPS Workshop at ARES 2026, LNCS, doi:10.1007/978-3-032-35576-8_3; **abstract only**, A1, Q32, Q34). Cited by deininger2026open as comparing open and frontier LLMs on WordPress-plugin web vulnerability detection [@deininger2026open, p. 3]. From the abstract:
=== G6
3:- **Second-pass verdict: narrowed.** deininger2026open now reports compute cost (USD) and energy (kJ) per true positive at realistic prevalence for 8 LLMs. What remains open is (a) the human triage term, i.e. analyst time spent on the false positives that come with each true positive, and (b) a quantified cost per true positive for the SAST and fine-tuned DL arms on the same targets.
5:  - **Most studies report no monetary cost.** 13 of our 20 primary studies report none [I, our count]. The seven that do are du, guo, li2026llm, shu, tan, xiong and deininger [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16; @shu2026evaluating, p. 42; @tan2026think, p. 10; @xiong2026sifting, p. 17; @deininger2026open, p. 7].
7:    - Per project: from $2.54 in the RepoAudit paper to $172.77 on average and $1,247.66 at most in li2026llm [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16] [V].
8:    - Thinking mode costs 2.7–4.4× the energy [@tan2026think, p. 10] [V]; in deininger2026open reasoning costs 4.5–12.1× more per task [@deininger2026open, p. 18] [V].
10:    - deininger2026open reports USD 0.003 (Gemma-3-4B) to 0.212 (Claude-Sonnet-5) and 3.7 to 119.6 kJ per true positive at 1:44 prevalence [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [V].
11:    - Flawfinder is given as ≈0 cost per true positive [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [V]. No cost per true positive is quantified for CodeBERT ("negligible inference cost") or for Cppcheck and Semgrep [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 11] [V].
12:    - Each LLM true positive comes with 25.6–41.9 false positives [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [V]. The paper notes that no triage workflow absorbs that alert volume [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [A], but analyst time is not costed [I]. At such ratios analyst time would plausibly dominate compute cost of a few cents per true positive [I].
13:    - Caveat for anyone reusing Table 5: its kJ per true positive for Qwen3-Coder-30B (4.0) and Llama-3.3-70B (44.8) uses FLOP estimates, not the measured per-task energy (88 J and 738 J) [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 14] [V]. Recomputed from the measured values these are about 8.8 and 34.9 kJ per true positive [I, from critical review D].
14:  - **Calls for audit-time measurement.** li2026llm calls for cost-aware designs [@li2026llm, p. 18] [A]. qin2026review recommends human-machine studies that record audit time per real vulnerability, and SAST-LLM systems evaluated by total audit cost [@qin2026review, p. 13] [A] (narrative review; not independent evidence).
16:  - **deininger2026open** (in corpus; see evidence above): compute cost and energy per true positive for LLMs; no triage term; SAST and DL arms not costed per true positive.
17:  - deininger2026open's related-work table rates Neef et al. (arXiv 2606.21397) and Dahiya et al. (arXiv 2605.23243) as giving partial treatment of cost [@deininger2026open, p. 3] [A]. Neither abstract mentions cost, a SAST arm or triage time (A1, A2; abstract only).
24:- Potential contribution: a decision-oriented metric for practitioners: dollars and analyst minutes per real vulnerability found. It would extend deininger2026open's compute-only USD per true positive with the term that probably dominates it [I].

content.content:
## Contradictions
<!-- Findings that disagree: which papers, what differs (data, method, population, metric), likely explanation (INTERPRETATION). Full discussion: reports/methodology-comparison.md §4. -->
- **C1 Fine-tuned vs GPT-4.** Fine-tuned AIBugHunter (F1 94%) and CodeBERT (87%) far exceed prompted gpt-4 (29%) on Big-Vul [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4], but GPT-4 CoT beats every fine-tuned model on pair-wise correctness on 564 PrimeVul pairs (12.94% vs ≤3.01%) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]. Differs in metric (F1 vs P-C), data (noisy random-split Big-Vul 1:20 vs de-duplicated time-split pairs) and model versions; Ding's own BigVul rows (F1 62.88–68.26%) agree with Fu [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. [I] Fine-tuned models exploit dataset artefacts rewarded by random splits [@risse2025top, p. 11]; on pairs all are below the 22.70% random reference, so the reversal reflects the benchmark more than the model family. Pass 2: on 1549 unpaired PrimeVul functions a fine-tuned CodeBERT-PrimeVul beats all 8 zero-shot LLMs (balanced accuracy 0.765 vs ≤0.711) [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17]; with an argmax decision rule the same detector looks like always-safe (0.500) despite ROC-AUC 0.845 [@deininger2026open, p. 11]. [I] A conservative threshold is consistent with Ding's fine-tuned models labelling both pair members benign in 84–88% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]; unpaired and pair-wise results must not be pooled.
- **C2 RepoAudit.** Own paper: 40 TP / 11 FP (78.43% precision), all 21 known bugs reproduced, $2.54 and 0.44 h per project [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8]. Independent study: 0/110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities [@li2026llm, p. 7], 92.77% SFDR on real-world projects [@li2026llm, p. 11], average $172.77 per project, max $1,247.66 [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Differs in targets (prior tools' bug reports vs ReposVul CVEs), version (old commits vs current HEAD; the 5 overlapping modules only in li's real-world set), metric (precision vs recall/SFDR), labeller (authors vs Codex), bug types and scale. [I] Dependence on source/sink API coverage (zero-token runs; API modelling explains 108/108 misses [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16]). Unresolved.
- **C3 LLM vs SAST.** LLMs win on 10 small C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10] and CASTLE C micro-programs [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; CodeQL beats the best LLM's accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]; at repository level LLMs detect more but flag up to 77.4% of functions [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7] (preprint), and general agents lead recall while specialised LLM detectors and SAST show near-zero recall on some CWEs and 75–100% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. Differs in language, unit, synthetic vs real code, and scoring leniency (location rule only for LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]; CASTLE prompt reveals scoring [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]). [I] Synthetic suites match SAST rules, small programs fit LLM context, real repositories defeat both: no single winner. Pass 2: on the same 1549 PrimeVul functions LLMs lead on balanced accuracy, but at 1:44 prevalence Flawfinder (6.2–13.4%) and Semgrep (26.0%, CI 5.7–66.9) are more precise than every LLM (2.3–4.6%), while Cppcheck sits in the LLM range [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 10]. [I] The families fail in opposite directions (LLMs over-flag, SAST finds little), so the ranking depends on the metric.
- **C4 Does reasoning reduce false positives?** For: reasoning models "consistently produced fewer false positives" [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14]; RepoAudit precision 82.35–88.46% with reasoning backbones [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 16]. Against: DeepSeek R1 166 FP vs GPT-4o 116 in CASTLE's own table [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; thinking raises F1 via recall with unchanged accuracy and turns negative under DA/MA [@tan2026think, p. 6; @tan2026think, p. 8]; reasoning LLMs near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 37]. [I] Holds for OpenAI o-series in some settings only. Pass 2, against: reasoning lowers DeepSeek-V3.2 specificity from 0.52 to 0.37 [@deininger2026open, p. 17; @deininger2026open, p. 20], while it helps frontier models' balanced accuracy. [I] Model-dependent.
- **C5 Class balance flips rankings.** Balanced REEF: fine-tuned GPT-4o + few-shot beats CodeT5P (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17]; imbalanced test: PLMs win (UniXcoder F1 0.4626 vs GPT-4o 0.4010) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @shu2026evaluating, p. 41]. yildiz F1 drops from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7]. [I] Balanced sets reward liberal flagging; balanced rankings do not transfer to deployment. Pass 2: deininger's precision ranking at 1:44 differs from its balanced-accuracy ranking [@deininger2026open, p. 8]; in tashenova changing how negatives are drawn flips the majority class and the direction in which the same Random Forest fails [@tashenova2026real, p. 9].
- **C6 IRIS hybrid.** IRIS+GPT-4 beats CodeQL on 120 Java CVEs (55 vs 27; AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03%) [@li2024iris, p. 8], but on real-world Java IRIS SFDR is 97.80% vs CodeQL 77.00% [@li2026llm, p. 12]. Not like-for-like (known CVEs vs new code; detections vs SFDR; labelling). [I] Hybrids may raise recall on benchmark CVEs while adding noise on unseen code. Open.
- **C7 Same model, same benchmark, different in-distribution score.** LineVul (CodeBERT) trained and tested on BigVul: F1 91.00 [@lu2025lab, p. 12] vs CodeBERT BV→BV F1 62.88 [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. Neither paper explains the 28-point gap. [I] Likely split and preprocessing differences (lu used LineVul's original pipeline [@lu2025lab, p. 8]); in-distribution BigVul numbers are not comparable across papers.
- **C8 Does a time-split fine-tuned detector survive?** CodeBERT-PrimeVul on PrimeVul's chronologically later test split keeps balanced accuracy 0.765 (F1 ≈ 0.15 at 1:44, our calculation) [@deininger2026open, p. 11], while BigVul/ICVul/Devign/Juliet-trained DL on post-May-2025 VentiVul falls to F1 3.47–8.65 [@lu2025lab, p. 13]. [I] Differences in dataset (VentiVul 2025 CVEs, Whole-File units), training data quality (PrimeVul vs BigVul) and threshold policy; unresolved.

## Agreements / converging evidence
- **G1 Realistic evaluation collapses performance (strong).** DL precision falls to 1–10% on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7]; code-LM F1 62.88–68.26% → 18.05–21.43% within PrimeVul and 1.91–5.82% cross-dataset [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]; LLM accuracy 10.5% lower on real-world than synthetic [@khare2025understanding, p. 5]; line-level F1 0.6641 → 0.3450 on 2024–25 code [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39]; statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8]. Surveys concur [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20]. Pass 2: on post-May-2025 CVEs at 1.97% prevalence, DL F1 3.47–8.65 and 7 of 12 LLM conservative F1 values fall below the all-positive F1 of 3.87% [@lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14]; at 1:44, LLM precision 2.3–4.6% vs flag-all 2.21% [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 17]; on real WordPress PHP CVEs best macro-F1 0.601 [@tashenova2026real, p. 8].
- **G2 Benchmark labels are noisy (strong).** Independent audits: 39–65% of vulnerable labels correct [@risse2025top, p. 8]; 24–36% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]; ReVeal 15% inconsistency [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 3]. (The 25% BigVul figure is Chen et al. via Ding — not independent.) Pass 2: only 48.8% of cleaned positive WordPress-PHP labels are genuine (single annotator, n = 400) [@tashenova2026real, p. 11].
- **G3 Prompted LLMs over-flag and cannot separate vulnerable from patched code (moderate).** GPT-4 two-shot labels both pair members vulnerable in 71.63% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]; "both vulnerable" is 40–95% of failures [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 8]; dual-agent flags 88.2% [@tan2026think, p. 7]; always-vulnerable rows among khare's best F1 [@khare2025understanding, p. 16]. Partly one dataset family (PrimeVul).
- **G4 SAST recall is low on real code, high only on synthetic suites (moderate).** Best single tools 30.0–44.4%, many 0% [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6]; CodeQL recall 6.00–34.29% C/C++ and 14.19% Java [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 9]; CodeQL 27/120 on CWE-Bench-Java [@li2024iris, p. 8]; CASTLE CodeQL 29%, SAST average 23% [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 12]; vs CodeQL accuracy 0.94 on Juliet Java [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- **G5 CodeQL on OWASP replicates across groups (moderate).** P 0.58 / R 0.96 / F1 0.72 [@khare2025understanding, p. 9] vs P 60.3% / R 97.0% / F1 74.4% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 11].
- **G6 Missing context is the shared failure cause (moderate).** All 151 truly vulnerable audited functions need external context [@risse2025top, p. 9]; context-type identification ≤41.33% [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 9]; API modelling explains 108/108 RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) misses [@li2026llm, p. 7]; 14.60% of FPs from truncated inter-procedural context [@li2026llm, p. 15].
- **G7 LLM filtering of SAST alarms trades large FP reduction for lost true positives (moderate).** du2026reducing removes 94–98% of false alarms with real-bug recall 0.75–0.88 [@du2026reducing, p. 8] (own method, Tencent authors, non-security bugs); xiong2026sifting FPR 6.3% with 22.25% miss rate [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18].
- **G8 Prompt-only LLMs trail adapted models (moderate).** Fine-tuned models beat prompted ChatGPT on Big-Vul [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4]; GPT-3.5 prompting detects 3.7–23.2% vs 89.2% fine-tuned CodeBERT [@zhou2024comparison, p. 10]; prompt-only LLMs near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
- **G9 LLM cost far exceeds SAST and varies by orders of magnitude (moderate).** RepoAudit averages $172.77 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16]; alarm filtering < $0.20 per alarm [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 17]; GPT-4o instruction tuning ~15× a PLM run [@shu2026evaluating, p. 42].
- **G10 Trivial baselines are competitive (moderate).** A one-feature token-count baseline matches or beats TF-IDF RF in 4/6 settings and is within 0.006 of the best neural model [@tashenova2026real, p. 8]; always-vulnerable F1 0.523 vs LLM F1 0.405–0.615 [@deininger2026open, p. 7]; all-positive F1 3.87% vs most LLM F1 on VentiVul [@lu2025lab, p. 14]; shu2026evaluating also reports all-vulnerable and all-clean dummy baselines [@shu2026evaluating, p. 11]. [I] Few papers report such baselines; most headline numbers are never compared to one.
- **G11 Cost per true positive (moderate, single study).** USD 0.003 (Gemma-3-4B) to 0.212 (Claude Sonnet 5) and 3.7–119.6 kJ per true positive at 1:44, excluding human triage of 25.6–41.9 false positives per true one [@deininger2026open, p. 8]; Qwen/Llama kJ/TP use FLOP estimates, not measured energy [@deininger2026open, p. 14].

# CASTLE: Benchmarking Dataset for Static Code Analyzers and LLMs Towards CWE Detection

- Authors: Dubniczky, Richard A.; Horvát, Krisztofer Zoltan; Bisztray, Tamás; Ferrag, Mohamed Amine; Cordeiro, Lucas C.; Tihanyi, Norbert
- Year / venue: 2025, Lecture Notes in Computer Science (book)
- DOI: 10.1007/978-3-031-98208-8_15 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-98208-8_15
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] To introduce CASTLE (CWE Automated Security Testing and Low-Level Evaluation), a compilable, balanced, line-labelled C micro-benchmark, and use it to compare static analyzers, formal verification (FV) tools and LLMs for CWE detection, together with a new metric, the CASTLE Score (p. 1–2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] RQ1: How do state-of-the-art static analysis tools, FV methods and LLM-based approaches compare in detecting C vulnerabilities? RQ2: Are combinations of tools more effective than a single tool? RQ3: What metrics can reliably show these differences? (p. 2).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Benchmark construction plus single-benchmark comparative evaluation of 25 tools/models (p. 6, p. 11).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] 10 LLMs prompted via OpenAI-style APIs with one system prompt ("professional security analyst"), returning JSON with severity, line, CWE, message and line content; the prompt states "You get 5 points for each vulnerability you find, but get -1 for all false positives" (p. 8–9). [V] LLMs: GPT-o3-Mini, GPT-o1, DeepSeek R1, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-Mini, Qwen 2.5 Coder Instruct 32B, Falcon 3 7B, Mistral Instruct 7B, Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B (Table 3, p. 11). No fine-tuning; zero-shot only.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Static analyzers with versions: CodeQL 2.20.1, GCC -fanalyzer 13.3.0, Snyk 1.1295.4, Semgrep Code 1.110.0, SonarQube 25.3.0, Coverity 2024.6.1, Cppcheck 2.13.0, Clang Analyzer 18.1.3, GitLab SAST 15.2.1, Splint 3.1.2, plus API-only Aikido, Jit, CodeThreat; FV tools ESBMC 7.8.1 and CBMC 5.95.1 (Table 3, p. 11). [V] ESBMC run with --overflow --no-unwinding-assertions --memory-leak-check --timeout 60 --multi-property (p. 12). [V] Tool combinations evaluated with a combination score (p. 10, p. 13). [I] No LLM + SAST/FV combination is evaluated (based on p. 11–13).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] 250 small C programs "crafted manually by cybersecurity experts"; each compiles (warnings allowed), single file, exactly one or zero vulnerabilities; vulnerable lines marked with `// {!LINE}` (p. 6–7).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 25 CWEs × 10 tests (6 vulnerable, 4 non-vulnerable) = 250 programs (150 vulnerable, 100 clean); 7–164 lines (mean 42, total 10,392); 1–8 functions; cyclomatic complexity 1–29 (mean 6.3); ~115,620 input tokens in total with the system prompt (p. 6).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] CWEs chosen mostly from the MITRE Top-25 of 2023–2024; 7 of the 25 CWEs are not in the 2024 Top-25 (e.g., CWE-253, -327, -362, -401, -617, -628, -843) (Table 2, p. 7). [V] Iterative expert validation; ambiguous cases mapped to higher-level CWE (p. 6–7). Number and selection of experts: not reported.
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] https://github.com/CASTLE-Benchmark (p. 1); wrappers public; intermediate vendor reports not shared (p. 9).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Free tools containerised in Docker with Python wrappers; closed-source tools (CodeThreat, Aikido) run via uploads to vendor dashboards/APIs with manual consistency checks (p. 8). [V] API-only tools and LLMs evaluated in February 2025 (p. 11). [V] LLM metadata and side-channel information removed before analysis (p. 7). [V] LLMs also return the code line content so that small line-number offsets could be adjusted during evaluation (p. 8). LLM temperature/sampling and model snapshot versions: not reported. Cost and runtime: not reported (only total token count, p. 6).
- Code availability: [V] Wrappers in the main repository (p. 9).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] TP, TN, FP, FN, precision, recall, accuracy (Table 3, p. 11). [V] CASTLE Score: per vulnerable test, correct detection scores 5 + Top-25 rank bonus (max 5) minus 1 per extra finding; per clean test with no report, 2 points; otherwise −(number of findings); missing a vulnerability with no report scores 0 (p. 9–10). Tools reporting nothing score 200; theoretical maximum 1,250 (p. 12). [V] Combination score: union of findings, TPs/TNs counted once, FP penalties summed (p. 10).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported. [A] Repeated evaluations deviate by less than 3% (p. 14); number of repeats not reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Static/FV tools (TP/TN/FP/FN, P/R/A, CASTLE): ESBMC 53/91/32/97, 62%/35%/53%, 661; CodeQL 45/79/49/112, 48%/29%/44%, 634; GCC Fanalyzer 41/76/93/109, 31%/27%/37%, 559; Snyk 26/82/42/124, 38%/17%/39%, 552; Semgrep Code 36/73/70/120, 34%/23%/36%, 541; CBMC 18/100/0/132, 100%/12%/47%, 536; SonarQube 43/68/135/107, 24%/29%/31%, 511; Aikido 481; Jit 478; Coverity 31/86/62/119, 33%/21%/39%, 425; Cppcheck 19/100/9/131, 68%/13%/46%, 406; Clang Analyzer 13/99/2/137, 87%/9%/45%, 381; GitLab SAST 36/67/240/120, 13%/23%/22%, 374; Splint −598 (1,027 FP); CodeThreat −692 (1,101 FP) (Table 3, p. 11).
2. [V] LLMs: GPT-o3-Mini 126/60/73/36, 63%/78%/63%, 977; GPT-o1 128/56/90/35, 59%/78%/60%, 962; DeepSeek R1 148/41/166/17, 47%/90%/51%, 956; GPT-4o 136/45/116/43, 54%/76%/53%, 954; GPT-4o-Mini 134/27/263/43, 34%/76%/34%, 761; Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B 114/31/224/49, 34%/70%/35%, 708; Falcon 3 7B 521; Mistral 7B 446; Gemma 2 9B 436; Llama 3.1 8B 83/22/337/80, 20%/51%/20%, 417 (Table 3, p. 11).
3. [A] CodeQL is the best SAST tool, finding "29% of the weaknesses in the code (45/150)" vs a 23% average among SAST tools; SonarQube also 29% but with 2.7× CodeQL's false positives (p. 12). [I] Labelled [A], not [V]: 45/150 = 30%, while 29% = 45/157 (CodeQL TP + FN in Table 3, p. 11); the same happens for GPT-o3-Mini, "126 out of the 150" (p. 14) but recall 78% = 126/162 (p. 11). The text therefore confirms the denominator problem in section 9.
4. [A] Reasoning models (o1, o3-mini) "consistently produced fewer false positives" than GPT-4o/4o-mini, which find more true positives (p. 14). [I] This holds for the OpenAI o-series only (o3-mini 73 FP, o1 90 FP vs GPT-4o 116, 4o-mini 263); DeepSeek R1, generally regarded as a reasoning model though the paper does not classify it, has 166 FP, more than GPT-4o (Table 3, p. 11). [A] LLMs "rival—and often surpass" classical static analyzers on compact code (p. 14).
5. [V] Best two-tool combination ESBMC + CodeQL scores 814, +153 over ESBMC alone (661), i.e., +23% vs ESBMC and +28% vs CodeQL (p. 13). [A] Combinations help when tools have complementary CWE coverage; overlapping tools lose score through added FPs (p. 13).
6. [A] FV tools have very few FPs (CBMC 0) but cannot detect non-formal issues such as SQL injection, path traversal or hard-coded credentials (p. 12).
7. [A] Smaller models (<6B parameters) often failed to produce well-formed JSON; models often found the right vulnerability with an offset line number (p. 8).
8. [A] In a preliminary test on a 400+ line program built by merging clean tests, LLMs reported more false positives and most failed to find one hidden injected vulnerability (p. 14). No numbers given.

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Micro-benchmark scope: single, isolated vulnerabilities; real software has cross-file flaws over many files (p. 14).
- [A] Lack of large code samples: LLM accuracy declines and false positives rise with code length; FV suffers state explosion; SAST scales better but has many FPs (p. 14).
- [A] Potential overfitting: fixed public tests could be targeted by vendors; dataset should be refreshed (p. 14).
- [A] LLM stochasticity, though repeated evaluations deviated less than 3% (p. 14).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Count inconsistencies in Table 3 (p. 11): there are 150 vulnerable programs, but TP + FN exceeds 150 for all 10 LLMs (154–179: o3-mini 162, o1 163, R1 165, GPT-4o 179, 4o-mini 177, Qwen 163, Falcon 154, Mistral 154, Gemma 158, Llama 163) and for 4 tools (CodeQL 45 + 112 = 157, Semgrep 156, GitLab SAST 156, Jit 155); the other 11 tools sum to exactly 150. The paper's own sentence "29% … (45/150)" (p. 12) shows it: 45/150 = 30%, 29% = 45/157. Recall therefore uses a denominator that is not the number of vulnerabilities (R1 recall 90% = 148/165, not 148/150), and accuracy is computed over finding counts rather than 250 programs. The counting rule for multiple findings per test is not explained. Exact recall/accuracy numbers should be quoted with this caveat.
- [I] The paper's own text is inconsistent on tool counts: "11 static code analyzers and 11 LLMs" (p. 3) vs 13 static + 2 FV + 10 LLMs (p. 1, p. 11).
- [I] Lenient LLM scoring: LLM line offsets were corrected using the returned line content (p. 8), a help not described for SAST tools; the prompt also mirrors the CASTLE scoring incentive (p. 9).
- [I] Synthetic, tiny, single-file programs (mean 42 lines) are ideal for LLM context windows and hard for tools tuned to real projects; the authors' own 400-line test suggests the ranking may flip on larger code (p. 14). This is the key external-validity caveat for RQ1.
- [I] The CASTLE Score is a new, author-defined weighting (bonus from Top-25 rank, 2 points per clean test, no penalty for silent misses) (p. 9–10). Its claim to be more reliable than precision/recall (p. 15) is not validated against any external criterion.
- [I] No per-CWE results table, so CWE-level strengths (RQ4) cannot be extracted beyond qualitative statements.
- [I] No LLM + static/FV hybrid is tested, though combination scoring would allow it.
- [I] LLM versions, temperature and costs not reported; closed models may change over time.
- [I] Funding partly from ZEISS Digital Innovation (p. 15); no conflict evident, noted for completeness. The authors filed ESBMC bug reports (p. 12) and co-authors' earlier FormAI dataset was labelled with ESBMC (p. 3); ESBMC ranks best among non-LLM tools here. Possible familiarity bias in configuring ESBMC (relaxed 60 s timeout, p. 12) is not discussed.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Author-built tests and author-defined metric; line-offset correction for LLMs only; possible bias toward ESBMC-friendly memory-safety CWEs. Newly written tests reduce pre-training contamination, but tests are now public (p. 1).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] C only; single-file micro-programs; 25 CWEs with 10 tests each; no real-world code.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] CASTLE Score weights are arbitrary; TP/FN accounting inconsistent with the 150-vulnerability ground truth.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] 6 vulnerable tests per CWE; differences of a few TPs between tools are within noise; no CIs; LLM run-to-run variance only summarised (<3%).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Dataset and wrappers public with tool versions (p. 1, p. 9, p. 11); LLM settings and API-tool versions missing.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: refresh the dataset or use dynamic test generation to prevent overfitting (p. 14); study scalability to large codebases for LLMs and FV (p. 15); select and combine tools to fit project needs (p. 15); LLMs as real-time guidance in code-completion frameworks (p. 1).
- Suggested by us [I]: extend CASTLE to multi-file and larger programs with the same line-level labels; test LLM + FV/SAST hybrids with the combination score; publish per-CWE results and fix TP/FN accounting.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: The broadest tool panel in our set (13 SAST incl. commercial Coverity, Snyk, SonarQube; 2 FV; 10 LLMs incl. reasoning models) on one controlled C benchmark with line-level ground truth. It supports "frontier LLMs beat SAST on small self-contained code", while its own preliminary large-file test and table inconsistencies limit how far this can be generalised. Useful for RQ2 as a contrast to real-world repo-level studies (e.g., zhou2024comparison).

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Top LLMs outscore all static and FV tools on CASTLE: GPT-o3-Mini 977, GPT-o1 962, DeepSeek R1 956, GPT-4o 954 vs ESBMC 661, CodeQL 634 | 11 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | LLM precision/recall: GPT-o3-Mini 63%/78%, GPT-4o 54%/76%, DeepSeek R1 47%/90%; small open models 20–28% precision | 11 | V | weak |
| RQ1 | SAST recall is low: CodeQL 29% (45 TP; 45/150 would be 30%, see RQ2 denominator row), SAST average 23%; high-precision tools have very low recall (Clang 87%/9%, CBMC 100%/12%) | 11–12 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Some SAST tools are unusable from noise: Splint 1,027 FP and CodeThreat 1,101 FP, giving negative CASTLE scores | 11, 13 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Benchmark is 250 hand-written single-file C programs (mean 42 lines), balanced 150/100, line-labelled; differs strongly from real-world repo-level setups | 6 | V | strong |
| RQ2 | Table 3 TP+FN exceeds the 150 vulnerable programs for all 10 LLMs (154–179) and 4 SAST tools (155–157), so reported recall/accuracy use inconsistent denominators (e.g., CodeQL "29% (45/150)" = 45/157) | 11–12 | I | moderate |
| RQ3 | Combining ESBMC and CodeQL raises the CASTLE score to 814 (+23% vs ESBMC); overlapping tools lose score through extra FPs; no LLM+tool hybrid tested | 10, 13 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Reasoning LLMs (o1, o3-mini) produce fewer FPs than GPT-4o/4o-mini; [I] not true for DeepSeek R1 (166 FP vs GPT-4o 116), so the claim holds for the OpenAI o-series only | 11, 14 | A | weak |
| RQ4 | FV tools miss non-formal CWEs (SQL injection, path traversal, hard-coded credentials) but have near-zero FPs; no per-CWE numbers reported | 12 | A | weak |
| RQ4 | LLM accuracy declines and FPs rise on a 400+ line merged program; most LLMs missed a single hidden vulnerability | 14 | A | weak |
| RQ5 | Open problems: LLM scalability to large codebases, line-level localisation, JSON reliability of small models, benchmark overfitting | 8, 14 | A | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "LLMs perform exceptionally well in the CASTLE dataset when identifying vulnerabilities in small code snippets. However, their accuracy declines, and hallucinations increase as the code size grows." (p. 1)

> "The best-performing SAST tool is CodeQL, which found 29% of the weaknesses in the code (45/150)" (p. 12)

> "most LLMs failed to detect it reliably, suggesting that these models’ effectiveness may taper off with increasing code length." (p. 14)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: whole paper read (pp. 1–18). Figures 1–3 are images; Fig. 2 combination labels are garbled in text extraction, so only the ESBMC + CodeQL combination (stated in text) is reported; other combination scores (697–758) are not attributed.
- Source version: arXiv v2 (2503.09433, 31 Mar 2025). Published version: book chapter in Lecture Notes in Computer Science, 2025 (DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-98208-8_15, from metadata; venue_kind "book", i.e., proceedings chapter). Metadata has no abstract; numbers could differ from the published chapter.
- Uncertainties: how multiple findings per test are counted in TP/FN (section 9); the exact LLM model snapshots; whether the published version corrected Table 3.

# Large Language Models Versus Static Code Analysis Tools: A Systematic Benchmark for Vulnerability Detection

- Authors: Gnieciak, Damian; Szandala, Tomasz
- Year / venue: 2025, IEEE Access (published)
- DOI: 10.1109/access.2025.3635168 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2025.3635168
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] A head-to-head quantitative and qualitative evaluation of three rule-based SAST tools (SonarQube, CodeQL, Snyk Code) and three LLMs on the GitHub Models platform (GPT-4.1, Mistral Large, DeepSeek V3) for vulnerability detection, measuring precision, recall, F1, latency and developer effort (p. 1–2).
- [A] Extends earlier work that compared GPT-3.5 Turbo and GPT-4o with SonarQube only (p. 4).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- Not reported as formal RQs or hypotheses. [A] Stated contributions: a unified benchmark and protocol, a quantitative comparison, qualitative insight from "thematic analysis of model rationales and tool reports", and practitioner guidance (p. 2).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Benchmark experiment: each tool/model runs once on each of 10 projects; every reported finding is manually checked against a reference list of known vulnerabilities (p. 6, p. 8).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] LLMs accessed via GitHub Models API through the authors' tool ProjectAnalyzer, which concatenates all project files (.cs, .csproj, .sln) into a single prompt and converts the JSON answer to SARIF (p. 5). [V] System prompt asks the model to act as "a static code analysis engine", lists 10 vulnerability types (SQLi, XSS, command injection, insecure deserialization, auth, hard-coded secrets, input validation, outdated libraries, weak crypto, file handling) and requests a JSON array with rule, message, path, line and column fields (p. 7). Zero-shot only; no fine-tuning.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] SonarQube, CodeQL, Snyk Code, all run with default configuration settings (p. 4, p. 8). [A] Snyk Code is described as using machine learning, i.e., a hybrid of ML and static analysis (p. 4, p. 9). Model and tool versions: not reported (GitHub Models endpoints named only by model name).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] 10 C# projects "prepared" for the study, each with "a random number of vulnerabilities" from six categories: SQL injection, XSS, hard-coded secrets, command injection, weak encryption algorithms, deprecated dependencies (p. 5). [A] The abstract calls them "real-world C# projects" (p. 1). [I] The methods text and sizes (3,145–5,317 characters) suggest small purpose-built projects with seeded vulnerabilities rather than real-world software (based on p. 5–6).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 10 projects, 3–10 files each, 3,145–5,317 characters, 1–13 vulnerabilities per project, 63 vulnerabilities in total (Table 3, p. 6). Unit of evaluation = reported finding matched to a known vulnerability.
- Sampling / selection method: [A] Project size (up to 10 files) chosen to match the most common change size in source-control history (p. 5). How vulnerabilities were chosen or inserted: not reported. CWE mapping: not reported.
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] ProjectAnalyzer code at https://github.com/Damian0401/ProjectAnalyzer (p. 1). [A] The abstract says an "open benchmark and JSON-based result harness" is released (p. 1); a separate dataset link is not given in the text.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Uniform execution environment; default configurations; execution time recorded in seconds to three decimals (p. 7–8). [V] LLM pricing (per 1M tokens): GPT-4.1 $2 in / $8 out; DeepSeek V3 $0.27 / $1.10; Mistral Large $2 / $6; context windows 1,047,576 / 64,000 / 32,000 tokens (p. 5–6). [V] SAST licence prices: SonarQube free Community / $65 per month Team; CodeQL $4 or $21 per user per month; Snyk Code from $25 per user per month (p. 5). Temperature, sampling settings, number of repetitions, hardware: not reported. Actual token usage or run cost: not reported.
- Code availability: [V] ProjectAnalyzer on GitHub (p. 1).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] TP = reported finding matching a known vulnerability (manually verified); FP = reported − TP; FN = known − TP; precision, recall and F1 computed per project and then averaged across projects (p. 6–7, p. 10). [V] Exception: for LLMs, wrong line/column locations were not counted against them (p. 6). [V] FP ratio (share of a tool's reports that are false) shown in Fig. 4 (p. 9). [V] Execution time per run (p. 7, p. 9).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported. [V] When a tool reported nothing on a project, its precision is recorded as 0.000 and enters the average (e.g., SonarQube S04, S05, S08, S10) (p. 9).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Mean precision / recall / F1 (macro over 10 projects): SonarQube 0.567 / 0.187 / 0.260; CodeQL 0.625 / 0.284 / 0.386; Snyk Code 0.686 / 0.523 / 0.546; GPT-4.1 0.757 / 0.877 / 0.797; Mistral Large 0.783 / 0.783 / 0.753; DeepSeek V3 0.723 / 0.847 / 0.750 (Table 13, p. 10).
2. [V] Raw counts (reported / TP over 63 known vulnerabilities): SonarQube 15 / 13; CodeQL 26 / 21; Snyk Code 57 / 42; GPT-4.1 74 / 55; Mistral Large 61 / 48; DeepSeek V3 70 / 52 (summed from Tables 4–5, p. 8). [I] Pooled over all projects this gives precision/recall/F1 of about 0.87/0.21/0.33 (SonarQube), 0.81/0.33/0.47 (CodeQL), 0.74/0.67/0.70 (Snyk), 0.74/0.87/0.80 (GPT-4.1), 0.79/0.76/0.77 (Mistral), 0.74/0.83/0.78 (DeepSeek) — our arithmetic from Tables 4–5; pooled SAST precision is higher than the macro averages suggest.
3. [A] The LLM advantage comes from higher recall, attributed to reasoning over broader code context (p. 1, p. 12).
4. [A] SonarQube and CodeQL have the lowest FP ratios; DeepSeek V3 has the highest FP ratio; Snyk Code lies between SAST tools and LLMs, explained by its hybrid ML + static approach (p. 9).
5. [V] Execution time per project: CodeQL 185.9–213.1 s; SonarQube 30.2–63.9 s; Snyk Code 13.9–29.3 s; GPT-4.1 3.5–17.8 s; Mistral Large 10.2–67.3 s; DeepSeek V3 5.8–29.9 s (Table 6, p. 9). [A] Project size in this range does not substantially affect runtime (p. 8).
6. [A] All LLMs identified the correct file but always reported an incorrect line/column location, likely due to BPE tokenisation (p. 11).
7. [V] LLMs hallucinated outdated-dependency findings for current library versions (e.g., Mistral Large flagged Microsoft.Data.Sqlite 9.0.5; GPT-4.1 flagged Newtonsoft.Json 13.0.3) (Table 14, p. 12).
8. [A] Recommendation: LLMs for early, broad triage during development; deterministic SAST for high-assurance audits in critical systems (p. 1, p. 12).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] LLMs cannot give correct line/column locations, which may preclude their use in SARIF-based pipelines (p. 11–12).
- [A] LLMs hallucinate findings such as outdated dependencies, which classical tools avoid through maintained deprecation lists (p. 11–12).
- [A] Higher sensitivity of LLMs comes with more false positives, which can cause alert fatigue (p. 11–12).
- [A] GPT-4.1 not publicly accessible, hence the use of GitHub Models for equal conditions (p. 5).
- No dedicated threats-to-validity section (p. 11).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Tiny, author-built benchmark: 10 projects, 63 vulnerabilities, each project ≤5,317 characters and ≤10 files (p. 6). The whole project fits easily in one prompt, which favours LLMs and does not reflect real repository scale. The "real-world" label in the abstract (p. 1) is not supported by the dataset description (p. 5).
- [I] Lenient scoring asymmetry: LLM findings count as TP even with wrong line/column locations (p. 6), while SAST tools are judged normally. This inflates LLM precision/recall relative to SAST.
- [I] Averaging choice penalises SAST: projects where a tool reports nothing get precision 0.000 and are averaged in (p. 9). Pooled counts (our calculation from Tables 4–5, p. 8) give SAST precision 0.74–0.87 vs LLM 0.74–0.79, and Snyk pooled F1 ≈ 0.70 near the LLMs. The FP-ratio ranking (DeepSeek highest) also depends on per-project averaging; pooled, GPT-4.1 has the most FPs (19) and Snyk's FP share (15/57) is similar to the LLMs'.
- [I] Single run per LLM with no temperature reported; LLM nondeterminism is not addressed, so results may not replicate.
- [I] Default SAST configurations only; e.g., SonarQube default profiles are not security-focused, and "deprecated dependencies" are normally the job of SCA tools rather than SAST, which disadvantages SonarQube/CodeQL on one of six categories.
- [I] Possible contamination: small synthetic C# examples of classic vulnerabilities resemble training data; not discussed.
- [I] Abstract claims measurement of "developer effort required to vet true positives" (p. 1) and contributions mention thematic analysis of rationales (p. 2); neither is reported as a measured result. Per-category (CWE) results are not given.
- [I] Run cost in dollars is not reported even though per-token prices are listed (p. 5–6).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Same authors created the projects, the prompt and the matching; lenient location rule for LLMs only (p. 6); no blinding of manual TP verification.
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] One language (C#), six vulnerability categories, very small projects; cloud-hosted frontier LLMs only; three SAST tools with default rules.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Detection without correct location is counted as success for LLMs; macro-average with zero-precision imputation distorts precision.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] N = 10 projects, 63 vulns, single runs, no tests or CIs; per-project F1 varies widely (e.g., S04 with 1 vulnerability).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Harness code public (p. 1); prompt published (p. 7); model versions, temperature and dataset link not reported.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: study prompt engineering effects; build a hybrid using classical tools and LLMs to prioritise and verify findings (p. 11).
- Suggested by us [I]: larger real-world C# corpora with CVE ground truth; strict location-aware scoring for all tools; repeated LLM runs; per-CWE breakdown; measured triage effort and cost per true positive.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4.
- How it informs our work [I]: A rare head-to-head comparison of commercial-grade SAST with frontier LLMs, reporting full precision/recall/F1 and runtime, in an under-studied language (C#). Its LLM-favourable result is useful but rests on a tiny, purpose-built benchmark and asymmetric scoring, so it should be treated as weak evidence and contrasted with larger real-world studies.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)

|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Macro mean F1: GPT-4.1 0.797, Mistral Large 0.753, DeepSeek V3 0.750 vs Snyk Code 0.546, CodeQL 0.386, SonarQube 0.260 on 10 C# projects (63 vulns) | 10 | V | weak |
| RQ1 | Macro mean recall: LLMs 0.783–0.877 vs SAST 0.187–0.523; macro precision LLMs 0.723–0.783 vs SAST 0.567–0.686 | 10 | V | weak |

> "All of the large language models tested were unable to determine it correctly." (p. 11)
