# Understanding the Effectiveness of Large Language Models in Detecting Security Vulnerabilities

- Authors: Khare, Avishree; Dutta, Saikat; Li, Ziyang; Solko-Breslin, Alaia; Alur, Rajeev; Naik, Mayur
- Year / venue: 2025, 2025 IEEE Conference on Software Testing, Verification and Validation (ICST) (published)
- DOI: 10.1109/icst62969.2025.10988968 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/icst62969.2025.10988968
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] To systematically evaluate how well pre-trained LLMs detect known security vulnerabilities across more datasets, languages, models, prompts and vulnerability classes than prior work, and to compare them with a static analyser (CodeQL) and deep-learning detectors (DeepDFA, LineVul) (p. 1–3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] RQ1: LLM performance across languages and datasets; RQ2: effect of prompting strategies; RQ3: variation across vulnerability classes (CWEs); RQ4: LLMs vs state-of-the-art static analysis; RQ5: LLMs vs state-of-the-art DL tools (Table I, p. 2). No formal hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Function/snippet-level binary classification benchmark on balanced samples, plus manual qualitative inspection of 20-sample subsets (p. 3–6).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] 16 pre-trained LLMs, "Instruct" variants where available: Qwen-2.5-Coder 1.5B/7B, CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B, DeepSeekCoder 7B/15B(v2)/33B, Llama-3.1 8B/70B, Qwen-2.5 14B/32B, Codestral-22B, Gemini-1.5-Flash, GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613) (Table V, p. 4). [V] Three prompts with a "security researcher" persona: Basic (any vulnerability), CWE-specific (target CWE named), CWE-DF (simulate source–sink–sanitizer dataflow analysis before the verdict) (p. 4, p. 14). [V] Few-shot and chain-of-thought were tried with GPT-4 on 100 samples and dropped as not better than CWE-DF (p. 4, p. 14–15). No fine-tuning of LLMs.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] CodeQL with official queries for the Top-25 CWEs, on synthetic datasets only (OWASP, Juliet Java, Juliet C/C++) because real-world projects need building (p. 7–8). [V] DeepDFA (GNN over CFG + dataflow facts) and LineVul (transformer) from DeepDFA's artifact, trained on Juliet C/C++, CVEFixes C/C++ (test samples excluded) or BigVul, 80/20 train/validation, tested on the 1,000 CVEFixes C/C++ samples, averaged over three runs (p. 9). CodeQL version: not reported.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] OWASP Benchmark (Java, synthetic), SARD Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ (synthetic), CVEFixes Java and C/C++ (real-world, method-level from NVD fix commits) (Table III, p. 3). [V] CVEFixes chosen because it has CVE/CWE metadata, is two-sided and multi-language (p. 3).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 5,000 code snippets: 1,000 per dataset, 500 vulnerable + 500 non-vulnerable; 25 CWEs (p. 1, p. 5; Table VI, p. 4). Unit = single method/snippet.
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Filtering: Top-25 CWE only, snippets ≤2,048 tokens, multi-file Juliet cases skipped, then random sampling (Table VI, p. 4; p. 5; p. 14). [V] Hints removed: comments stripped, identifying names (e.g., "CWE80_XSS…", "owasp") anonymised (p. 5, p. 14). [V] CVEFixes labels: pre-fix vs post-fix versions of methods changed in fix commits (p. 14).
- Data availability (public? link?): source datasets public (p. 3); the authors' sampled subsets and evaluation code: not reported (no link in this version).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] OpenAI ChatCompletions API (GPT-3.5/4), Gemini API, Hugging Face for open models on a cluster with A100, A6000 and RTX 2080 GPUs; temperature 0, max 1,024 output tokens, top-1 prediction, default other parameters (p. 5). [V] Single run per benchmark (p. 10). [A] CWE-DF "is costlier since it generates more tokens" (p. 4). Token counts, monetary cost, runtime: not reported.
- Code availability: not reported in this version.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 as standard classification metrics (p. 3–4). [V] Balanced accuracy per CWE for RQ3/RQ4, only CWEs with ≥10 samples, best prompt per model and dataset (p. 6–7). [V] RQ1 reports the best accuracy/F1 per model per dataset across prompts (p. 5).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported; [A] "significantly" is used descriptively (p. 1); standard-deviation bars across models in Fig. 2 (p. 5).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Best model+prompt per dataset averages 62.8% accuracy; bests are Llama-3.1-70B (CWE) 76% on Juliet Java, Qwen-2.5-14B 65% on Juliet C/C++, CodeLlama-13B 60% on OWASP, Gemini-1.5-Flash 57% on CVEFixes Java, Qwen-2.5-32B 56% on CVEFixes C/C++ (p. 5). [A] Mean F1 0.71 (p. 1–2). [I] Both headline means are averages of the best value per dataset in Table XII (p. 16): accuracy (0.60+0.76+0.57+0.65+0.56)/5 = 0.628; F1 (0.70+0.79+0.67+0.73+0.67)/5 = 0.712. Two of the five best F1s (CVEFixes Java and CVEFixes C/C++, 0.67) come from "always vulnerable"-type rows (P 0.50, R 0.99–1.00).
2. [V] Best accuracies on synthetic datasets are 10.5% higher on average than on real-world datasets (p. 5).
3. [A] Performance does not improve with scale: Qwen-2.5-14B/32B beat GPT-x on real-world data; only GPT-x and Llama-3.1-x improve with size on ≥3 datasets (p. 5).
4. [V] CWE-DF raises average F1 over CWE and Basic prompts on real-world datasets by up to 0.18 (CVEFixes C/C++) and 0.14 (CVEFixes Java), with lowest variance across models (p. 5). [V] Basic prompt names an incorrect CWE in >60% (Java) and >53% (C/C++) of samples (p. 6; Table VII).
5. [V] Manual inspection (20-sample subsets): CWE-DF identifies correct sources/sinks in 18/20 and sanitizers in 16/20 real-world Java samples; on wrongly predicted Juliet C/C++ samples, sources/sinks/sanitizers are correct in 17/20 but unsanitized flows wrong in 12/20 (p. 6).
6. [V] CWE-wise: best on self-contained vulnerabilities — CWE-78 (Llama-3.1-70B 64% CVEFixes Java, 78% CVEFixes C/C++), CWE-787/125 in Java (Llama-3.1-8B/GPT-4 up to 89%/84%), CWE-476 (DSCoder-7B 63–88%), CWE-89 (GPT-3.5 70% on CVEFixes Java), CWE-79 (Qwen-2.5-32B 66–67%); poor on CWE-862 and on C/C++ out-of-bounds (<53% for GPT-4/Llama-3.1-8B; no LLM >60%) (p. 7).
7. [V] CodeQL vs best LLM per synthetic dataset (A/P/R/F1): OWASP 0.63/0.58/0.96/0.72 vs CodeLlama-13B 0.60/0.58/0.74/0.65; Juliet Java 0.94/0.92/0.95/0.94 vs Llama-3.1-70B 0.76/0.71/0.89/0.79; Juliet C/C++ 0.72/0.99/0.44/0.61 vs Qwen-2.5-14B 0.65/0.60/0.89/0.72 (Table VIII, p. 9). CodeQL has higher accuracy on all three; the LLM has higher F1 only on Juliet C/C++ (p. 8). [I] On OWASP both CodeQL (A 0.63, R 0.96, F1 0.72) and the best LLM (A 0.60, F1 0.65) are close to the always-vulnerable baseline (A 0.50, F1 0.667); the LLM's F1 is below it (Table VIII, p. 9).
8. [V] LLMs beat CodeQL on CWE-22, CWE-78, CWE-476, CWE-416 on ≥2 of 3 datasets (e.g., DSCoder-7B +24% on CWE-416 Juliet C/C++; +12% on CWE-476 Juliet Java); CodeQL beats LLMs on CWE-190 by 11% (Juliet Java) and 21% (Juliet C/C++) (p. 8). [A] CodeQL misses some cases because its queries are narrow (e.g., CWE-78 query handles execl but not _execvp) (p. 8).
9. [V] DL tools on CVEFixes C/C++ (A/P/R/F1), Table IX (p. 10): DeepDFA trained in-distribution 0.51/0.55/0.17/0.23, on Juliet 0.53/0.53/0.65/0.58, on BigVul 0.52/0.52/0.76/0.62; LineVul in-distribution 0.59/0.58/0.65/0.61, on Juliet 0.50/0.50/0.91/0.64, on BigVul 0.50/0.63/0.01/0.02; Qwen-2.5-32B (CWE-DF, no training) 0.56/0.54/0.81/0.65. DL F1 on CVEFixes therefore ranges 0.02–0.64, and in-distribution LineVul has higher accuracy than Qwen (0.59 vs 0.56) (p. 9–10). Trained on BigVul, both reach ≥0.98 accuracy on BigVul (p. 10). [A] DL tools do not generalise across datasets; LLMs preferable for low inference overhead and explanations (p. 9–10). [I] Qwen's F1 of 0.65 is below the 0.667 F1 of always answering "vulnerable" on this 50/50 set, as are all DL F1s, so the F1 comparison does not show that any of these tools beats the trivial baseline (based on Table IX, p. 10).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Choice of LLMs and datasets may bias results; may not generalise to other languages or datasets (p. 10).
- [A] Single runs; GPT-3.5/GPT-4 may be non-deterministic even at temperature 0 (p. 10).
- [A] Possible bugs in evaluation code and errors in manual analysis, mitigated by multiple co-authors' review (p. 10).
- [A] Multi-file samples and snippets >2,048 tokens excluded due to prompt size (p. 5, p. 14).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Headline F1 is close to a trivial baseline: on 50/50 balanced data, always answering "vulnerable" gives P = 0.50, R = 1.00, F1 = 0.67, and many configurations show exactly this pattern (e.g., CodeLlama-7B, CodeLlama-13B, CodeLlama-34B and DSCoder-15B with CWE-DF: A 0.50 / P 0.50 / R 1.00 / F1 0.67 on most datasets, Table XII, p. 16). The mean F1 of 0.71 therefore says little: it is the mean of the best F1 per dataset (0.70, 0.79, 0.67, 0.73, 0.67; Table XII, p. 16), and two of those five bests are always-vulnerable-type rows (CVEFixes Java 0.50/0.50/1.00/0.67; CVEFixes C/C++ CodeLlama-34B CWE-DF 0.50/0.50/0.99/0.67). On real-world CVEFixes data, no configuration's F1 exceeds 0.67, i.e. none clearly beats the trivial 0.667. Accuracy (~50–60%) is the more honest signal.
- [I] Best-of-48 selection: RQ1 and RQ4 report the best model+prompt per dataset chosen after seeing test results (p. 5, p. 8), which favours LLMs against a single CodeQL configuration.
- [I] CodeQL is compared only on synthetic Juliet/OWASP data, where CodeQL queries are well-tuned, and LLM–CodeQL comparison on real-world code is absent (p. 7–8). This limits RQ1/RQ4 conclusions for real code.
- [I] Balanced 50/50 evaluation does not reflect real-world prevalence of vulnerable code; precision would drop sharply at realistic ratios.
- [I] Data contamination: Juliet, OWASP and CVEFixes are public and predate the LLMs' training cut-offs; not discussed beyond identifier anonymisation (p. 5, p. 14).
- [I] CVEFixes method-level labels are known to be noisy (fix-commit heuristic); label quality is not assessed. The appendix sentence labelling methods "in the fix commit and the parent commit … as vulnerable and non-vulnerable, respectively" (p. 14) reads reversed relative to the usual convention; likely a wording error.
- [I] Table V lists "DSCoder-15B" as deepseekcoder-v2-15b with size "33B" (p. 4), an internal inconsistency.
- [I] The abstract's statement that LLMs report higher accuracies than CodeQL refers to specific CWEs only; overall CodeQL wins on accuracy on all three synthetic datasets (p. 1 vs p. 8).
- [I] No cost or runtime data, so trade-offs for RQ3 cannot be assessed.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Post-hoc best-configuration selection; possible pre-training contamination; DL tools trained with 80/20 split but tested on the same 1,000-sample set as LLMs (CVEFixes test samples excluded from training, p. 9).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Function-level snippets only, no inter-procedural/multi-file context; two languages; Top-25 CWEs; balanced sampling.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Binary verdict ignores whether the predicted CWE or location is right (Basic prompt names wrong CWE >53–60% of the time, p. 6); F1 on balanced data inflated by "always yes" behaviour.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] 1,000 samples per dataset is reasonable, but per-CWE analysis uses as few as 10 samples (p. 7); no significance tests or CIs; single runs.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Prompts fully given (p. 14–15) and model versions listed (p. 4); sampled subsets and code not linked in this arXiv version.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: neuro-symbolic techniques combining LLM reasoning with logical reasoning engines and static analyzers (p. 11); use LLMs to infer specifications (sources, sinks, sanitizers) that static analysis then reasons over (p. 6, p. 8–10).
- Suggested by us [I]: evaluate CodeQL and LLMs together on real-world code at realistic prevalence; report trivial baselines; test the proposed LLM-specification + static-analysis hybrid directly.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: Peer-reviewed (ICST 2025), multi-dataset study that covers all three families (LLM, SAST via CodeQL, DL via DeepDFA/LineVul). It shows CodeQL still wins overall on synthetic suites while LLMs win particular CWEs, and that LLM F1 on balanced data can be near-trivial. It is a key source for RQ4 (CWE-specific strengths) and for the "LLM finds specs, static analysis reasons" hybrid idea in RQ3/RQ5.

# Comparison of Static Application Security Testing Tools and Large Language Models for Repo-level Vulnerability Detection

- Authors: Zhou, Xin; Tran, Duc-Manh; Le-Cong, Thanh; Zhang, Ting; Irsan, Ivana Clairine; Sumarlin, Joshua
- Year / venue: 2024, arXiv (preprint) — **not peer-reviewed**
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2407.16235 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16235
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] To compare SAST tools with LLMs for detecting vulnerabilities in whole repositories, understand the pros and cons of each family, and explore combining them (p. 1).
- [A] Introduces a "repo-level" detection task: find the vulnerable functions among all functions of a repository rather than only among functions in files touched by a fix commit (p. 2–3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] RQ1: How effective are SAST tools and LLMs? RQ2: Which is more effective, SAST tools or LLMs? RQ3: To what extent can combining multiple SAST tools or LLMs improve detection? (p. 7).
- No formal hypotheses (p. 7).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Empirical benchmark study; 15 SAST tools and 12 open-source LLMs evaluated on the same held-out test sets for Java, C and Python (p. 5, p. 7).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] LLMs: 4 lightweight (<1B) models — CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, CodeT5, UniXcoder — with full fine-tuning; 8 large (3.8B–8B) decoder models — CodeLlama-7B, Llama3-8B, CodeQwen-7B, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, Mistral-7B, Phi3-3.8B, StarCoder-7B, StarCoder2-7B — with LoRA fine-tuning (PEFT), zero-shot, chain-of-thought ("Let's think step by step") and few-shot (2 examples) prompting (p. 4–5). [V] Repositories are split into functions with Tree-sitter, each function classified separately, and predictions aggregated per repository (p. 3).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] SAST, all free/open-source: Java — CodeQL, Contrast Codesec Scan, Horusec, Insider, SpotBugs, Semgrep, SonarQube CE; C — Flawfinder, Cppcheck, Infer, CodeChecker, CodeQL; Python — Bandit, Dlint, DevSkim, CodeQL, Graudit, Semgrep (p. 4). [V] Commercial LLMs excluded from the main study because of cost and non-reproducibility (p. 4); a small side experiment uses gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 (p. 9). [V] Ensembles: union of all SAST tools per language; voting over 12 fine-tuned LLMs at >50%, >2/3 and >80% thresholds (p. 8–9). [I] No ensemble combining SAST and LLM outputs is actually run, despite the abstract and conclusion wording (based on p. 8–9 vs p. 1, p. 11).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Java from Li et al. (SAST study for Java), C from Lipp et al. (static C analyzers study), both real-world CVEs whose repositories were re-downloaded; new Python dataset built from NVD 2002–2023 entries linked to GitHub fix commits (p. 3).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] Java 50 projects / 87 CVEs / 3,986,848 functions (vulnerable ratio 0.008%); C 6 projects / 85 CVEs / 1,181,556 functions (0.009%); Python 78 projects / 98 CVEs / 312,045 functions (0.18%) (p. 3). Unit of detection = CVE within a repository; unit of marking = function.
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Repositories kept only if downloadable via the GitHub API (Java) or per the original authors' instructions (C); Python projects that errored during SAST scanning were omitted (p. 3). [V] Vulnerable functions = pre-fix versions of functions changed by the fix commit; all other functions labelled non-vulnerable (p. 3–4). [V] Random 8:1:1 train/validation/test split; SAST and LLMs evaluated on the same test sets (p. 5). Test-set sizes: not reported. [I] Detection ratios move in steps of 12.5 (Java), 11.1 (C) and 10.0 (Python) points in Table 3 (p. 6), implying test sets of about 8, 9 and 10 vulnerabilities.
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Code and data are "publicly accessible" (p. 10); no link given in the text.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Fine-tuning on a balanced training set (all vulnerable functions + equal number of random non-vulnerable functions), 20 epochs, batch size 8, best snapshot on a balanced validation set; LoRA r = 8, α = 16; Hugging Face; Ubuntu 22.04 with an NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU; models capped at 8B parameters due to compute (p. 4–5, p. 7). [V] Prompt: "If the following code snippet has any vulnerabilities, output Yes; otherwise, output No" with code markers (p. 4). [V] ChatGPT side experiment: 1:100 vulnerable:clean sample, temperature 0 (p. 9). SAST tool versions and rule configurations: not reported. Runtime and monetary cost: not reported.
- Code availability: [A] stated public, no URL (p. 10).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Vulnerability detection ratio = detected vulns / all vulns; Scenario 1 (S1): at least one vulnerable function of the CVE flagged; Scenario 2 (S2): all vulnerable functions flagged (p. 5). [V] Marked function ratio = flagged functions / all functions, used as an approximation of the false-positive rate because only 0.008–0.18% of functions are vulnerable (p. 5). [V] Precision and F1 deliberately not computed because unknown vulnerabilities may exist (p. 5).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported; single runs, no variance or CIs. [V] A rank-sum heuristic (rank by S2 + rank by marked ratio) picks the "best" approach (p. 8).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] SAST detection is low: many tools detect 0% (CodeQL, Contrast, Insider, SpotBugs, SonarQube for Java; Flawfinder, Cppcheck, CodeChecker for C; CodeQL, Graudit for Python) and SAST tools mark only 0.2%–5.2% of functions (p. 6–7). Best per text: Horusec Java S1 37.5%; CodeQL C 44.4% S1 / 33.3% S2; DevSkim Python 30.0% / 20.0% (p. 7). Infer (C) 11.1% / 11.1% with 0.9% marked; Semgrep Python 10.0% / 10.0% with 0.6% marked (p. 6).
2. [V] LLMs detect much more but flag many functions: up to 100% S1 / 87.5% S2 in Java (fine-tuned Llama3, 21.8% marked), 100% / 88.9% in C (fine-tuned CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, UniXcoder; 25.6–44.6% marked), 90% / 90% in Python (fine-tuned CodeT5, 50.5% marked) (p. 6). LLMs mark 8.3–77.4% of functions in Java, 3.5–70.1% in C, 14.9–73.4% in Python (p. 7).
3. [V] Fine-tuning beats prompting for large LLMs: in Java, PEFT models average 73.4% (S1) / 51.6% (S2) detection with 19.4% marked vs 52.1–55.0% marked for prompting (p. 7). Fine-tuned lightweight models detect 10.6% / 9.1% more (S1 / S2) than fine-tuned large ones in Java but mark 43.2% more functions (p. 7). [I] All three figures are relative gains, not percentage points: Table 3 Java means are 81.25 vs 73.44 (S1, ≈ +7.8 points), 56.25 vs 51.56 (S2, ≈ +4.7 points) and 27.8 vs 19.4 marked (p. 6; PEFT CodeLlama marked read as 8.3, see section 9).
4. [A] By the rank-sum metric, best approaches are fine-tuned DeepSeek-Coder (Java), UniXcoder (C) and Llama3 (Python); the best choice depends on language and tolerated marked ratio (p. 8).
5. [V] Union of SAST tools raises detection: Java S1 37.5% → 50.0% (marked 1.7% → 4.3%); C 44.4% → 55.6% S1 and 33.3% → 44.4% S2 (marked 5.2% → 7.2%); Python 30.0% → 50.0% S1 and 20.0% → 40.0% S2 (marked 4.5% → 7.7%) (p. 8).
6. [V] Voting over 12 fine-tuned LLMs (>2/3) cuts the marked ratio by 61.7% (Java), 74.6% (C), 40.9% (Python) relative to the LLM average while keeping detection near the best single LLM; >80% voting gives marked ratios 0.8–9.2% but S2 detection only 0–37.5% (p. 9).
7. [A] Combined LLMs are best for Java; combined SAST tools are best for C and Python (p. 9).
8. [V] CWE view (languages merged, SAST union vs union of the 2 best LLMs): CWE-119 best detected (LLM group 100%), CWE-476 second; CWE-835 and CWE-89 detected by neither group (p. 8).
9. [V] ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125, 1:100 sample, averaged over languages): S1 3.7% zero-shot, 3.7% CoT, 23.2% few-shot, marked 1.3–10.8%; fine-tuned CodeBERT 89.2% S1 / 35.7% marked and fine-tuned Llama3 67.4% / 20.1% in the same setting (p. 10).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Undiscovered vulnerabilities may exist in the benchmarks; the study only measures detection of known vulnerabilities (p. 10).
- [A] Possible data leakage from LLM pre-training; argued to be minor because prompting performs worse than fine-tuning (p. 10).
- [A] Commercial LLMs excluded from the main study due to cost (p. 4, p. 9); models limited to ≤8B parameters by compute (p. 4).
- [A] Only generic LLM techniques used, no specialised designs (p. 10).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Very small test sets: detection ratios are multiples of ~10–12.5 points (Table 3, p. 6), so each language result rests on about 8–10 CVEs; one CVE moves a ratio by 10+ points. No variance, repeated splits or CIs. Most cross-tool differences are therefore statistically unreliable.
- [I] Typesetting defect in Table 3 (dropped leading digits), not conflicting results. Table 3 prints Horusec Java S1 = 7.5, CodeQL C = 4.4 / 3.3, DevSkim Python = 0.0 / 0.0 and truncated cells ".0", ".3", ".5" (p. 6; present in the rendered PDF), while the text gives 37.5, 44.4 / 33.3 and 30.0 / 20.0 (p. 7). The text values are consistent with the table's other cells: ".3" (PEFT CodeLlama, Java marked) must be 8.3, the lower bound of the stated Java range "8.3% to 77.4%" (p. 7), and it reproduces the stated PEFT mean of 19.4% (p. 6–7); ".5" (PEFT Llama3, C marked) matches the lower bound 3.5 of "3.5% to 70.1% in C" (p. 7); 7.5 is not a multiple of the 12.5-point Java step. Two more cells fall below the stated ranges and are probably affected too: C Starcoder2 PEFT marked 0.3 (< 3.5) and Python DeepSeek-Coder few-shot marked 4.9 (< 14.9) (p. 6–7). We quote best-SAST numbers from the text.
- [I] Abstract and conclusion say that ensembling "the SAST tools and LLMs" mitigates both families' drawbacks (p. 1, p. 11), but experiments only combine SAST with SAST and LLM with LLM (p. 8–9). This paper gives no direct evidence on SAST+LLM hybrids.
- [I] Asymmetric comparison: LLMs were fine-tuned on 80% of the same CVE distribution (random CVE-level split, so the same project can appear in train and test), while SAST tools run untuned. Project-level leakage is not discussed.
- [I] The marked function ratio is a proxy for false positives, not an FPR; with no precision/F1, numbers cannot be pooled with precision/recall-based studies.
- [I] SAST versions, rule sets and configurations not reported; 0% results (e.g., CodeQL on Java and Python) may reflect configuration or build issues rather than tool capability.
- [I] Fine-tuned models train on balanced data but are tested on extremely imbalanced repositories, which plausibly explains the high marked ratios.
- [I] The PDF running header uses an "ESEC/FSE'23" template although this is a 2024 preprint (p. 2); it is not evidence of peer review.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Random CVE-level split without project grouping; label noise from the fix-commit heuristic (all other functions labelled clean, p. 3–4); pre-training leakage acknowledged by the authors (p. 10).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Only ≤8B open models and free SAST tools; the C dataset has only 6 projects (p. 3); no commercial SAST and no frontier LLMs beyond a small GPT-3.5 test.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] S1 counts a CVE as detected if any one of its functions is flagged, which favours tools that flag many functions; the marked ratio only approximates FPR.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] ~8–10 test CVEs per language, single run, no tests; many comparisons across 15 tools × 12 LLMs × 4 adaptations.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Hyper-parameters reported (p. 5, p. 7); code/data claimed public without a link (p. 10); SAST configuration missing.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: shift from function-level to repo-level detection (p. 10); reduce LLM marked ratios via filtering untrustworthy predictions, adding repository structure context, better prompting or ensembles (p. 10); combine LLMs and SAST tools more effectively (p. 10–11).
- Suggested by us [I]: re-run with project-grouped splits, multiple seeds and larger test sets; measure precision on manually triaged samples; actually test SAST+LLM hybrids (e.g., LLM triage of SAST alerts). Based on the limitations in section 9.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: One of the few studies comparing many SAST tools with many fine-tuned and prompted LLMs on the same real-world, multi-language data. It supports the recurring pattern "SAST = low recall, few alarms; LLM = high recall, many alarms", but its small test sets, a typesetting defect in Table 3 and preprint status make it moderate-to-weak evidence.

# LLM-based Vulnerability Detection at Project Scale: An Empirical Study

- Authors: Li, Fengjie; Jiang, Jiajun; Chen, Dongchi; Xiong, Yingfei
- Year / venue: 2026, IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering (published)
- DOI: 10.1109/tse.2026.3742453 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/tse.2026.3742453
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). Our PDF is arXiv:2601.19239v2 (25 Sep 2026, stamp on p. 1), not the IEEE version of record; page numbers and possibly some numbers may differ from the TSE copy.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
Systematically evaluate specialized project-scale LLM-based vulnerability detectors against general-purpose coding agents and traditional static analyzers on (a) known vulnerabilities and (b) current real-world projects, explaining their false positives and measuring their cost [A] (p. 1, p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: How effective are LLM-based methods at detecting known vulnerabilities in a controlled benchmark? [V] (p. 3)
- RQ2: How reliable are they on real-world projects/modules, in terms of false discovery rates? [V] (p. 3)
- RQ3: What are the root causes of false positives? [V] (p. 4)
- RQ4: What is the overhead (tokens, money, time) of project-scale LLM detection? [V] (p. 4)
- No formal hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: comparative empirical benchmark study, plus qualitative FP root-cause taxonomy (open coding, double coding) and LLM-assisted (Codex) labelling with stratified manual validation [V] (p. 6, p. 11, p. 13).
- Approach / model / intervention (Table I, p. 4) [V]:
  - Specialized LLM-based: RepoAudit (multi-agent; Claude Sonnet 3.5 / GPT-5.4; C/C++; CWE-401/416/476), KNighter (LLM-synthesised Clang Static Analyzer checkers; o3-mini / GPT-5.4; C/C++), IRIS (LLM-inferred sources/sinks + CodeQL; GPT-4 / GPT-5.4; Java; CWE-022/078/079/094), LLMDFA (multi-agent dataflow; GPT-4 / GPT-5.4; Java; CWE-078/079), INFERROI (LLM intent inference + CFG; GPT-4 / GPT-5.4; Java; CWE-772) (p. 4, p. 5).
  - General agents: Codex (GPT-5.4) and Claude Code (Claude Sonnet 4.6), all CWEs, internet search disabled (p. 4, p. 7).
  - Each specialized method run with its original backbone and with GPT-5.4 to separate model from workflow effects (p. 4).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: traditional SAST — CodeQL (48 selected rules, C/C++ and Java), Semgrep (59 rules, C/C++ and Java), SpotBugs + Find Security Bugs (21 patterns, Java), Clang Static Analyzer CSA (12 checkers, C/C++) [V] (p. 4, p. 7). Rules were manually curated to the target CWEs; all severities treated equally [V] (p. 7). No deep-learning (fine-tuned/GNN) detectors and no prompt-only/RAG function-level methods (excluded because they do not produce repository-level warnings) [V] (p. 4). LLMxCPG excluded (needs local fine-tuning) [V] (p. 4).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): controlled dataset from ReposVul (C/C++), CWE-Bench-Java (Maven projects only) and JLeaks (50 randomly sampled resource leaks); all cases manually checked for validity and successful compilation [V] (p. 5). Real-world dataset: 24 actively maintained projects/modules with historical vulnerabilities in the studied CWEs (e.g. Linux subsystems, ImageMagick, Vim, gpac, bitlbee; OpenOLAT, Spark, DSpace, XStream, Jenkins, Keycloak, Tika, xwiki, ActiveMQ, RxJava, jsoup) [V] (p. 5, p. 6).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 265 known vulnerabilities — C/C++: CWE-401 50, CWE-416 25, CWE-476 35; Java: CWE-022 49, CWE-078 11, CWE-079 28, CWE-094 17, CWE-772 50 [V] (p. 6). 24 projects/modules sized 1,715 to 6,033,855 LOC [V] (p. 6). Up to 300 warnings sampled per tool per project → 6,442 warnings; 5,896 FPs classified; 355 warnings manually coded to build the taxonomy (>150 person-hours) [V] (p. 6, p. 11, p. 13).
- Sampling / selection method: for ReposVul, the three repositories with most cases per CWE (to limit build effort); 8 CWEs chosen by tool support and benchmark availability [V] (p. 5). 21 of 24 real-world commits postdate the August 2025 knowledge cutoff of GPT-5.4 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 [V] (p. 5). Several C/C++ modules come from the same Linux commit [A] (p. 18). No power analysis.
- Data availability (public? link?): artifacts (scripts, prompts, taxonomy labels, statistics) at https://github.com/Feng-Jay/LLM4Security [V] (p. 2).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: released replication packages of each specialized tool with hyper-parameters from the original papers; no extra timeouts or token/money budgets [V] (p. 6). Default RepoAudit configuration; IRIS/LLMDFA/INFERROI use their own LLM-generated API lists; KNighter checkers generated from 18 bug-fixing patches from its original study [V] (p. 7). General agents via official CLIs with built-in tools/skills, internet off [V] (p. 7). Official OpenAI/Anthropic APIs; local server with dual Xeon 6388, 512 GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04.6 [V] (p. 7). Each LLM configuration run once [A] (p. 18).
- Controlled-dataset TP rule: a vulnerability counts as detected if the tool reports the labelled vulnerable program point; FPs are warnings in known vulnerable files that do not match the known data-flow pattern (IRIS protocol) [V] (p. 5, p. 6).
- Real-world labelling: Codex labels each sampled warning TP/FP with access to the repository; validation on up to 5 TPs + 5 FPs per tool per repo (197 TPs, 424 FPs) [V] (p. 11).
- Code availability: yes, project homepage above [V] (p. 2). Appendices A–C (FP examples, rule lists, detailed cost statistics) are referenced but are not in our 20-page PDF (p. 7, p. 13, p. 15).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - Recall = TP/(TP+FN) and Precision = TP/(TP+FP) on the controlled set, following prior studies [V] (p. 5, p. 6).
  - #Reports, #Files, #Sampled FPs and SFDR = #Sampled FPs / #Sampled Reports on real-world projects, because ground truth is unknown there [V] (p. 6).
  - Input/output tokens, USD and end-to-end minutes per project/module; cost and minutes per warning [V] (p. 6, p. 15, p. 16).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): no significance tests between tools. Labelling accuracy estimated with stratified sampling, normal approximation and finite-population correction at the 95% level [V] (p. 11, p. 13); the intervals themselves are not printed in the text we have.

## 7. Key findings
1. C/C++ controlled set: general agents average recall 59.55% (131/220) and precision 32.19% (131/407); KNighter detects 0 vulnerabilities in all three CWEs; RepoAudit with its original backbone (Claude Sonnet 3.5) detects 0 of 110 (0 TPs among 40 warnings: 0 warnings on CWE-401, 33 on CWE-416, 7 on CWE-476), and RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) detects 2 (CWE-476 recall 5.71%) — [V] (p. 7, Table IV).
   - Table XII lists a minimum of 0.00K input tokens and $0.00 for both RepoAudit variants on the real-world projects — [V] (p. 16). [I] So on at least one project RepoAudit made no LLM call at all; this fits the authors' finding that incomplete API modelling explains all 108/108 RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) misses (p. 7), i.e. sources/sinks were never matched. Relevant to the guo2025repoaudit tension (§9).
2. C/C++ per CWE (Table IV): CWE-401 Codex R 68.00% / P 41.98%, Claude Code R 80.00% / P 40.00%, CodeQL R 6.00% / P 14.29%, Semgrep and CSA 0%; CWE-416 Codex R 40.00%, Claude Code R 36.00%, CodeQL/Semgrep/CSA 0%; CWE-476 Codex R 62.86%, Claude Code R 45.71%, CodeQL R 34.29% with 1,110 warnings (P 1.08%) — [V] (p. 7).
3. Java controlled set: Codex average recall 63.87% (99/155), Claude Code 81.94% (127/155); CodeQL 14.19%, Semgrep 6.67%, SpotBugs 14.84%; LLMDFA (GPT-5.4) finds 1 vulnerability; INFERROI (GPT-5.4) reaches 66.00% recall on CWE-772 vs CodeQL 10.00% and SpotBugs 6.00% — [V] (p. 9, Table VI p. 10).
4. Java precision is low for most tools (e.g. CWE-022: IRIS GPT-4 6.30%, Semgrep 0.29% from 2,075 warnings, SpotBugs 1.76%, Codex 58.73%, Claude Code 37.29%) — [V] (p. 10, Table VI).
5. Swapping in GPT-5.4 barely changes recall of specialized methods but raises some precision (IRIS CWE-078 6.06% → 20.00%; INFERROI 15.74% → 20.50%) — [V] (p. 9). The authors conclude that the workflow, not the model, limits recall (e.g. RepoAudit GPT-5.4 vs Codex on the same model) — [A] (p. 9).
6. Incomplete API modelling and incomplete candidate exploration explain 108/108 (RepoAudit GPT-5.4), 97/110 (KNighter GPT-5.4), 40/44 (Codex) and 40/45 (Claude Code) missed C/C++ vulnerabilities — [V] (p. 7). With perfect allocation/deallocation API specs on CWE-401, recall rises: RepoAudit 0 → 48%, Codex 68 → 90%, Claude Code 80 → 96%, CodeQL 6 → 56% — [V] (p. 8, Table V).
7. Vulnerabilities missed by general agents sit in larger files than detected ones (Fig. 4 C/C++, Fig. 6 Java) — [V] (p. 9, p. 10). The authors attribute this to file size and complexity, and say IRIS and INFERROI are largely unaffected because they reason over compact representations such as CFGs — [A] (p. 8, p. 10).
8. LLM-based tools contribute most unique detections; traditional tools add few unique ones (CodeQL at most 3 unique on CWE-022) — [V] (p. 9, p. 10, Fig. 5).
9. Real-world C/C++ (Table VII): overall SFDR RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) 92.77%, KNighter (o3-mini) 81.25%, Codex 9.09% (2.44 warnings/project), Claude Code 74.07%, CodeQL 86.01% (752.67 warnings/project; 6,345 on gpac), Semgrep 100.00%, CSA 85.51% — [V] (p. 11). GPT-5.4 versions: RepoAudit 95.41%, KNighter 95.56% (Table VIII) — [V] (p. 11).
10. Real-world Java (Table IX): IRIS (GPT-4) 97.80% SFDR with 232.42 warnings/project, LLMDFA 100.00%, INFERROI 96.40%, Codex 31.82% (1.47 warnings/project), Claude Code 81.82%, CodeQL 77.00%, Semgrep 92.71%, SpotBugs 86.21%; traditional tools emit warnings in only about half of projects — [V] (p. 12). IRIS with GPT-5.4 drops to 78.73% (Table X) — [V] (p. 12).
11. Codex labels were 94.36% accurate on 621 manually validated warnings (population-weighted 98.16%); Codex FP-reason labels 87.76% accurate on 425 cases (weighted 92.52%) — [V] (p. 11, p. 13).
12. FP root causes: incorrect program-point classification B1 = 63.33% (3,734/5,896) and truncated interprocedural context A1 = 14.60% (861/5,896); LLM tools additionally show incorrect control flow (A2), missed sanitizers/guards (D1, >15% in 7 of 12 LLM settings) and prompt deviations (C1) — [V] (p. 15, Table XI p. 14). CodeQL's largest FP causes are A1 35.80% and path-insensitivity D3 20.17% — [V] (p. 14).
13. Cost (Table XII): RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) up to 225,493.97K input and 38,078.26K output tokens and $1,247.66 for one project, average $172.77; LLMDFA (GPT-4) average $61.60 and 2,000 min per Java project (max 4,638 min); IRIS (GPT-4) average $2.59, 213.44 min; INFERROI average $11.62–$12.99; KNighter $0.34–$2.36; Codex $5.38 / 14.80 min; Claude Code $9.67 / 13.19 min per project. SAST average runtimes 0.64 (Semgrep) to 60.92 (CSA) minutes, no token cost — [V] (p. 16).
14. Per warning: Codex $2.93 and 8.1 min, Claude Code $1.77 and 2.4 min; LLMDFA >$24 and >800 min per warning — [V] (p. 15, p. 16).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Controlled evaluation counts warnings about other, unlabelled genuine vulnerabilities as FPs (p. 18).
- [A] Each LLM configuration run once; nondeterminism may affect results (p. 18).
- [A] Taxonomy and labels involve expert judgement; large-scale labels partly come from Codex and may contain model bias (p. 18).
- [A] Pretraining contamination possible for both datasets; post-cutoff commits may retain older code; sessions showed no explicit reliance on CVE data (p. 18).
- [A] Tool selection, two languages (C/C++, Java), 8 CWEs; several Linux modules share one repository/commit; no concurrency or type-confusion bugs; may not generalise to Rust, Go, TypeScript or multi-language projects (p. 18).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Codex (GPT-5.4) is both an evaluated detector and the main TP/FP labeller and FP-reason classifier. Codex has by far the lowest SFDR (9.09% C/C++, 31.82% Java). Validation was stratified (≤5 TPs + ≤5 FPs per tool per repo), so a judge that favours its own reports is only partly ruled out; per-tool labelling accuracy is not reported. Based on p. 11 and Tables VII/IX.
- [I] The low SFDRs of general agents rest on very few warnings (Codex: 2.44 × 9 ≈ 22 C/C++ and 1.47 × 15 ≈ 22 Java warnings), so they are imprecise; no per-tool confidence intervals are shown. Based on Tables VII and IX (p. 11, p. 12).
- [I] Controlled-set precision only counts FPs inside known vulnerable files, so it is not project-wide precision and is not comparable with SFDR or with precision in other papers. Based on p. 6.
- [I] SAST rule sets were curated by the authors (48/59/21/12 rules); other rule choices could change SAST recall and FP counts. Based on p. 7.
- [I] The controlled benchmark uses public CVEs that likely predate model training; general agents' high controlled recall may partly reflect memorisation even without explicit lookup. The post-cutoff real-world set gives no recall, so recall on unseen code is not measured. Based on p. 5, p. 18.
- [I] No deep-learning (fine-tuned) detectors are compared: informs LLM vs SAST, not LLM vs DL. Based on p. 4.
- [I] Backbones differ across tools (Claude Sonnet 4.6 vs GPT-5.4 vs GPT-4), so agent-vs-specialized comparisons mix workflow and model effects, partly controlled by the GPT-5.4 re-runs. Based on Table I (p. 4).
- [I] Documented tension with guo2025repoaudit (RepoAudit's own evaluation); both sides are confirmed in the texts and neither is a replication of the other. Based on the pages cited below.
  - Effectiveness. guo: RepoAudit (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) reproduces all 21 previously reported bugs and finds 19 new ones, 40 TPs / 11 FPs, precision 78.43%, on 15 C/C++ projects [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7, p. 8]. li: RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) detects 0/110 and RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) 2/110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities (p. 7); real-world SFDR 92.77% as a 9-project average (p. 11).
  - Cost. guo: average $2.54 and 0.44 h per project, maximum $18.15 (icu) [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7, p. 8]. li: average $172.77, maximum $1,247.66 per project, and over 800 min maximum runtime (p. 15, p. 16). The project behind the $1,247.66 maximum is not named in the main text; details are deferred to Appendix C (p. 15), which our PDF lacks.
  - Dataset. guo's targets are bug reports of prior tools [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7]. li's controlled set is ReposVul CVEs from "the three repositories with the most cases" per CWE, and li does not name those repositories (p. 5). The targets overlap only with li's *real-world* set, where recall is not measured: linux/sound, linux/mm, linux/drivers/net, linux/drivers/peci and ImageMagick (Table III, p. 6; [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7]). For 3 of these 5 the bug type differs: ImageMagick is NPD in guo but CWE-401 in li, linux/driver(s)/net is MLK vs CWE-416, and peci is UAF vs CWE-476. Sizes differ at every shared target. For example, linux/sound is 1,378,262 LoC in guo vs 1,253,234 in li, and guo analyses ImageMagick/MagickCore (242,555) while li analyses the whole ImageMagick repository (680,878). guo's "linux/driver/net" (914,025) is closer in size to li's linux/net (962,143) than to li's linux/drivers/net (3,924,621), so the module mapping is unclear. On li's linux/net, RepoAudit emits 3 warnings with an SFDR of 66.67% (Table VII, p. 11). On the other shared projects li's RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) emits 0 warnings (linux/sound, linux/mm, ImageMagick), 1 FP (linux/drivers/net) and 3 FPs (peci) (Table VII, p. 11).
  - Commit. guo analyses the versions used by the earlier works, and its new bugs are "in historic versions" [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7, p. 8]. li uses recent commits 6093a68 (Linux) and 3bf1076 (ImageMagick) (p. 6). guo's 4 Linux known bugs are all intra-procedural [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 8], and li notes that RepoAudit was evaluated on only 4 intra-function Linux cases (p. 7).
  - Metric. guo reports precision on the tool's own reports and reproduction of 21 known bugs. li reports recall on CVEs (controlled set) and SFDR (real-world set).
  - Labeller. guo does not describe how RepoAudit's own reports were judged TP/FP; only the Infer/CodeGuru reports are said to be labelled manually [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 14]. li used Codex labels with stratified manual validation (p. 11).
  - Scale. guo's projects average 251 KLoC, and its 4 Linux modules took only 1–35 prompts and $0.03–$0.86 each [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7, p. 8]. li runs RepoAudit with no time or money budgets (p. 6) on modules up to 3,924,621 LOC; it emits 77 warnings on gpac and 374 on bitlbee (Tables III and VII, p. 6, p. 11). guo itself says cost depends on the number of source elements [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 9].
  - Explanation (ours). Target selection, code version, bug-type mapping, project scale and metric all differ, so the results are not directly comparable. RepoAudit made no LLM call on at least one project in li (0.00 tokens, Table XII, p. 16), and guo's Linux runs used very few prompts. Together with li's API-modelling analysis (p. 7), this points to source/sink coverage as one plausible mechanism for both the low recall and the cost spread.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): LLM self-labelling (see 9); pretraining contamination acknowledged (p. 18); single runs (p. 18); different backbones per tool (p. 4).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): C/C++ and Java only, 8 CWEs, 24 projects with several from one Linux commit (p. 18); tools limited to publicly available, runnable ones (p. 4).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): SFDR measures false alarms among sampled warnings, not missed vulnerabilities; controlled precision is file-restricted (p. 6); all SAST severities counted equally (p. 7).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no significance tests between tools; small warning counts for some tools; no run-to-run variance.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): good — artifacts, prompts and rule lists released (p. 2, p. 7); API model versions may change.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: combine flexible agents with program-analysis support such as path constraints, IRs and validators (p. 17); integrate LLMs with formal analysis/symbolic execution (p. 17); evidence-grounded API-role/specification inference with iterative validation (p. 17); explicit modelling of ownership, sanitizers, error paths and resource lifecycles (p. 17); structured multi-agent or self-verification for prompt compliance (p. 17); cost-aware designs — hierarchical/incremental analysis, caching, adaptive LLM invocation, cheaper models (p. 18); broader languages and CWE classes (p. 18).
- Suggested by us [I]: an independent (non-evaluated) judge or full manual labelling for warning triage; repeated runs with variance; LLM vs DL vs SAST on the same post-cutoff projects with recall measured via newly disclosed vulnerabilities.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: one of the few head-to-head project-scale comparisons of LLM detectors and SAST (CodeQL, Semgrep, SpotBugs, CSA) on the same targets, with recall, precision/SFDR and cost. It shows "LLM vs SAST" depends heavily on the LLM workflow: general agents beat SAST on recall, specialized hybrids (IRIS, INFERROI, KNighter) often do not. Gives concrete cost data for RQ3 and an FP taxonomy shared by both families for RQ5.

28	## 1. Research objective
29	[A] To benchmark open-weight against frontier LLMs on function-level vulnerability detection, treating monetary cost and energy as "first-class axes alongside detection quality" (p. 1). The study also calibrates the LLM results against non-LLM reference points (static analysers and learned detectors) "to gauge absolute difficulty" (p. 2). [A] The authors claim the conjunction is new (a security task, a five-model open roster, and cost and energy as per-task axes), stating "We make no claim to be first on any single one of these axes" (p. 3).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- [V] No numbered RQs. Contributions are framed as (p. 2):
33	  - a cost- and energy-aware open-vs-frontier benchmark on label-clean PrimeVul with non-LLM reference points;
34	  - evidence on the quality–efficiency Pareto frontier;
35	  - an account of what can and cannot be measured for closed API models.
36	- [I] Implicit questions:
37	  1. Are open-weight LLMs competitive with frontier LLMs in quality?
38	  2. Are they more cost- and energy-efficient?
39	  3. How do LLMs compare with SAST and fine-tuned detectors at realistic prevalence?
40	
41	## 3. Methodology
42	- Research design: [V] Empirical benchmark of binary function-level detection ("does this C/C++ function contain a vulnerability?") on a fixed stratified PrimeVul sample (p. 4). Additional analyses (pp. 9–20):
43	  - re-scoring at the natural 1:44 prevalence;
44	  - configuration-matched families A/B/C;
45	  - prompt, sample-draw and run-to-run robustness;
46	  - a reasoning-vs-direct replication across two measurement epochs.
47	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Eight LLMs prompted zero-shot through a unified OpenAI-compatible API gateway (p. 4, Table 2). [V] The gateway is **not named** (pp. 4, 29).
48	  - **Frontier:** Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.1, Gemini 3.1 Pro (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`); active parameters assumed ~100B for the energy estimate.
49	  - **Open-weight:** DeepSeek-V3.2 (~37B active), GLM-5 (~32B active), Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-Coder-30B (3B active MoE), Gemma-3-4B.
50	  - [V] Pinned providers and precision: DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 at GMICloud FP8; Llama-3.3-70B at DeepInfra FP8; Qwen3-Coder-30B at SiliconFlow FP8; Gemma-3-4B at DeepInfra bf16 (p. 29, Table A2).
51	  - [V] Main configuration: direct answer, reasoning disabled where permitted. Gemini cannot disable reasoning (HTTP 400) (p. 4, p. 29).
52	  - [V] Prompt: a security-reviewer persona; answer YES/NO first, then an optional explanation (p. 28). A lenient parser counts unparseable outputs as parse failures, not "safe" (p. 4, p. 29).
53	- Baselines or comparison conditions:
54	  - [V] **Trivial baselines:** always-safe and always-vulnerable (p. 7, Table 4); always-flag at 1:44 prevalence (p. 8, Table 5).
55	  - [V] **SAST arm** (p. 6, p. 10, Table 7): Flawfinder 2.0.20 (lexical), Cppcheck 2.21 (flow-sensitive), Semgrep 1.175 with community C and security-audit rulesets (pattern plus intraprocedural taint). A function is flagged if any finding reaches a swept severity threshold.
56	  - [V] **DL arm:**
57	    - CodeBERT fine-tuned on Devign (off the shelf, cross-dataset, argmax, 512 tokens) (p. 6);
58	    - CodeBERT (125M) fine-tuned on PrimeVul's training split, with the threshold selected on the validation split (p. 10–11).
59	  - [V] **CodeQL was not run.** PrimeVul functions are isolated snippets with no build, so no CodeQL database can be built (p. 10–11).
60	
61	## 4. Dataset and sample
62	- Data source(s): [V] PrimeVul test split (C/C++): 24,788 functions after loading, 549 vulnerable — "a realistic 1:44 class ratio" (p. 4).
63	  - [I] This differs from the PrimeVul test split recorded in ding2025vulnerability (695 vulnerable / 25,216 benign) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 6]. The paper does not explain the difference beyond "after loading" (p. 4); filtering or de-duplication on load is plausible but not reported.
64	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] N = 1549 functions: all 549 vulnerable plus 1000 seeded-random safe functions (p. 4). [I] Prevalence in the evaluated sample is 35.4% (549/1549). This is **not** 50/50, although the text once calls it "balanced by construction" (p. 8). [V] The effective N per model is 1526–1549 because parse failures are excluded (p. 6).
65	- Sampling / selection method:
66	  - [V] Label-stratified sample fixed by seed (p. 4).
67	  - [V] Two further near-disjoint safe pools (<6% overlap) were drawn for robustness (p. 19).
68	  - [V] LLM inputs were truncated to 8000 characters. This affects 105/1549 functions and 87/549 (15.8%) of the vulnerable ones (p. 4).
69	  - [A] "The two non-LLM baselines" see the untruncated function and are therefore "if anything, advantaged" on long inputs (p. 4). [V] But the CodeBERT-Devign baseline uses "inputs truncated to 512 tokens" (p. 6); the input length of CodeBERT-PrimeVul is not reported (pp. 10–11).
70	  - [I] The untruncated claim can hold only for the SAST tools. CodeBERT's 512-token window is shorter than the LLMs' 8000-character budget, so on long functions CodeBERT is, if anything, disadvantaged — which strengthens rather than weakens its win over the LLMs (basis: p. 4, p. 6; CodeBERT-PrimeVul's limit inferred from the architecture, not reported).
71	  - [V] All CVEs date from 2008–2022 and predate the models' training cutoffs (p. 24). [V] The PrimeVul training split contains no evaluated function or function body (up to whitespace) (p. 10, p. 25).
72	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Released on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.21391073): harness, configurations, sampled function IDs, price snapshot, energy sweep, baseline scores and aggregated results (p. 26). [V] PrimeVul is fetched from its original authors by script; the fine-tuned checkpoint is regenerable by script (p. 26).

74	## 5. Experimental setup
75	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
76	  - [V] Harness and decoding: a test-driven harness with 82 automated tests; temperature 0, seed 12345, one generation per item; output budget 64 tokens in the matched configuration (256 for two frontier models in the first epoch) (p. 6, p. 29).
77	  - [V] Cost: computed from logged input/output tokens × list price at a pinned provider, with gateway fallbacks disabled (p. 5).
78	  - [V] Provider price dispersion: up to 14.4× for DeepSeek-V3.2 (USD 0.209–3.000 per million input tokens) (p. 5, Table 3).
79	  - [V] Energy (p. 5):
80	    - FLOP estimate E ≈ 2·N_active·T·ε for API-served models;
81	    - measured with the NVML energy counter on a dedicated NVIDIA H200 for locally servable open models (concurrency 1, idle-subtracted "active" energy);
82	    - plus a concurrency sweep c = 1/8/32/64 (p. 14, Table 9).
83	  - [V] Latency: client-side under concurrency 10, so it conflates queueing (p. 30).
84	  - [V] Statistics: stratified paired bootstrap of balanced-accuracy differences (20,000 resamples, seed 12,345) with Holm correction over a 9-comparison primary family and a 15-comparison strict family (p. 6, p. 28).
85	- Code availability: [V] The harness and configurations are released (p. 6, p. 26).

87	## 6. Evaluation metrics
88	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
89	  - [V] **Balanced accuracy** is the primary metric, because accuracy is dominated by the always-safe classifier (0.646 accuracy, above every LLM) and both trivial classifiers score exactly 0.5 on it (p. 6).
90	  - [V] MCC and F1 are also reported (p. 6).
91	  - [V] Deployment metrics at 1:44 prevalence are derived from the prevalence-invariant TPR/FPR (p. 8, Table 5):
92	    - precision; false positives per true positive (FP/TP);
93	    - alerts and found vulnerabilities per 1000 functions;
94	    - **USD per true positive** and **kJ per true positive**.
95	  - [V] Elicited 0–100 confidence gives ROC-AUC where usable. VD-Score is declined because the coarse score grids cannot reach its 0.5% FPR point (p. 9–10).
96	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):
97	  - [V] Paired bootstrap 95% CIs and Holm-adjusted p for open-vs-frontier gaps (p. 27, Table A1).
98	  - [V] Wilson-based 95% CIs on precision at deployment prevalence for the non-LLM baselines (p. 10, Table 7).
99	  - [V] Robustness: Spearman rank correlation across prompts and draws (p. 19, Table 13).
100	  - [V] Output-budget effects are tested with a paired bootstrap (p. 16, Table 10).

190	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
191	- [A] Energy is measured for only some open models; frontier energy rests on an untested active-parameter assumption and is reported as a sensitivity range (p. 23).
192	- [A] Configuration asymmetries: Gemini cannot run without reasoning; two frontier models needed larger output budgets in the main run (p. 24).
193	- [A] Latency is confounded by queueing (p. 24).
194	- [A] Training-data contamination: all CVEs are 2008–2022 and may appear in pre-training; a recall gradient by CVE year is "consistent with some memorization"; absolute scores "may be optimistic"; a post-cutoff restriction is planned (p. 24).
195	- [A] The fine-tuned CodeBERT-PrimeVul detector is in-distribution (trained on PrimeVul's own training split) while the LLMs are zero-shot; the authors call this "not an unfair comparison" but note the different prerequisites (several thousand labelled vulnerable functions vs none) (p. 11).
196	- [A] One prompt, one draw and one generation in the headline table; variation across datasets and task formulations remains unbounded (p. 24).
197	- [A] Serving-layer dependence (p. 24–25):
198	  - price spread up to 14×;
199	  - two silent serving faults: billed empty outputs, and a reasoning flag ignored with HTTP 200;
200	  - quality is robust to provider and precision for Llama (0.599–0.609).
201	- [A] CodeQL cannot be applied to unbuildable function snippets (p. 25).
202	- [A] Scope: one dataset, one task formulation, function level only; other languages and statement-level localisation are future work (p. 25).
203	- [A] "No result here should be read as evidence that function-level vulnerability triage is ready for independent use" (p. 26).

205	## 9. Limitations we identified
206	- [I] **Internal inconsistencies from revision** (the paper went through at least one major review round, p. 1, pp. 16–19):
207	  - Gemma-3-4B is said to be incompatible with the local vLLM/CUDA build, so its energy is FLOP-estimated (p. 6, p. 15). Yet Table 9 reports a measured concurrency sweep for Gemma (p. 14), and the abstract says three open models were measured (p. 1), while p. 5 says two.
208	  - The limitations list says a fine-tuned PrimeVul detector "is the remaining gap" (p. 25), but Section 4.4 reports exactly such a detector (p. 10–11).
209	  - The reasoning cost multiplier is "2.5 to 7.6 times" on p. 24, which refers to the earlier-epoch comparison of Section 4.9 (p. 20); Section 4.9 gives no cost table, so that range cannot be checked. Cite Table 12's 4.5–12.1× (p. 18) instead.
210	  - The sample is called "balanced by construction" (p. 8) although it is 35.4% positive (p. 4).
211	  - p. 2 says "every model we tested raises roughly twenty-six false alarms per true finding", but Table 5 gives 25.6–41.9 FP/TP; 25.6 is the best model only (p. 8). p. 21 attributes "roughly twenty-six" to "the best model".
212	  - p. 23 says the best open models "dominate the frontier on both the quality and the efficiency axes", whereas p. 21 says the data "do not support a general claim of quality dominance", and DeepSeek's lead over Claude in Family C is not significant (p = 0.081) (p. 17).
213	  - p. 4 speaks of "two non-LLM baselines (Section 3.4)", but Section 3.4 lists four non-LLM detectors (p. 6).
214	  - These are reporting slips, not evidence of wrong numbers, but readers should cite table values rather than prose.
215	- [I] **The SAST arm is weak by design for C/C++.** Flawfinder, Cppcheck and Semgrep community rules on isolated functions, with no CodeQL, Infer or commercial tools (p. 10–11). The comparison is LLM vs lightweight function-level SAST, not vs semantic whole-program SAST.
216	- [I] Contamination and the in-distribution vs zero-shot asymmetry are author-stated (§8, p. 11, p. 24). Our addition: both cut in different directions — contamination may inflate the LLM scores, while the asymmetry favours CodeBERT — so the size of CodeBERT's lead over zero-shot LLMs on genuinely unseen code is unknown.
217	- [I] **Cost per TP excludes triage.** With 25.6–41.9 FP per TP (p. 8), analyst time would dominate compute cost (cents per TP). The paper's USD/TP therefore understates the practical cost per confirmed vulnerability by a large factor.
218	- [I] **Unnamed gateway** and preview model identifiers (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`, p. 29) limit long-term reproducibility. The service drift of up to 0.06 between epochs (p. 20) shows API results are time-stamped observations.
219	- [I] **Function-level, C/C++ only** — no repository context. The truncation at 8000 characters affects 15.8% of positives (p. 4).
220	- **AI-assisted writing and code.** [V] The authors used DeepL Translator and ChatGPT (GPT-5.5, OpenAI) "to translate words, phrases, and passages from German into English", and Claude (Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, Anthropic) "to assist with drafting and revising portions of the text and with writing Python code"; "no figures, data, or images were AI-generated or fabricated" (p. 27). [V] The harness is covered by 82 automated tests (p. 6).
221	  - [I] Both assisting vendors (OpenAI, Anthropic) also supply evaluated models (GPT-5.1, Claude-Sonnet-5; p. 4). The disclosure and the test suite reduce the concern; we note it for transparency, not as a conflict. Our own analysis pipeline is also Claude-based, which readers may wish to weigh when judging our reading of Claude results.

223	## 10. Threats to validity
224	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
225	  - [V] Train/test separation for CodeBERT-PrimeVul is verified: no evaluated function or body is in training (p. 25).
226	  - [V] Thresholds are tuned on validation, not test (sweeping on test would give 0.777 vs the reported 0.765) (p. 11).
227	  - [V] Contamination is not controlled but is measured as a recall gradient by CVE year (p. 24).
228	  - [V] Epoch drift is handled by within-epoch comparisons (p. 16–18).
229	  - [V] Parse failures are excluded, not recoded (p. 27).
230	- External (generalisability of sample/context):
231	  - [V] One dataset (PrimeVul), C/C++, function level (p. 25).
232	  - [I] It is unclear whether results hold for repository-level detection or other languages.
233	  - [I] Model versions are a 2026 snapshot.
234	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):

## Large Language Models Versus Static Code Analysis Tools: A Systematic Benchmark for Vulnerability Detection

> **Takeaway:** On ten small C# projects with planted security flaws, three chatbot-style LLMs found far more flaws than three standard code scanners (mean F1 0.75–0.80 against 0.26–0.55). The test set is tiny and the scoring was more lenient for the LLMs, so treat this as weak evidence.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Damian Gnieciak, Tomasz Szandala |
| Year | 2025 |
| Venue | IEEE Access (journal) |
| Status | Peer-reviewed. Our copy is the arXiv version (2508.04448, v1), so numbers may differ slightly from the published article. |
| Identifier | DOI 10.1109/access.2025.3635168 |
| Paper type | Empirical benchmark (head-to-head comparison) |
| Relevance to us | High — RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4 |

### In plain words
A security vulnerability is a mistake in code that an attacker can exploit. One classic way to find such mistakes is static application security testing (SAST). SAST tools read the source code without running it and apply fixed rules, such as "user input must not flow into a database query". A newer way is to ask a large language model (LLM), a chatbot-style AI trained on huge amounts of text and code, to review the code.

This paper puts three well-known SAST tools (SonarQube, CodeQL and Snyk Code) against three LLMs (GPT-4.1, Mistral Large and DeepSeek V3). All six look at the same ten small C# projects. The LLMs win clearly on the authors' headline numbers. But the paper also shows two practical problems: the LLMs never gave the right line number, and they sometimes reported problems that did not exist.

### How they did it
The authors built a tool called ProjectAnalyzer. It pastes every file of a project into one prompt and asks the LLM to act as "a static code analysis engine" [@gnieciak2025large, p. 7]. The prompt lists ten vulnerability types and asks for a structured answer. This was zero-shot: the models got no examples and no extra training. The SAST tools ran with their default settings [@gnieciak2025large, p. 8]. Each tool or model ran once per project. The authors then checked every reported finding by hand against a list of the known flaws [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6].

The main measures are precision, recall and F1. Precision is the share of a tool's warnings that are real flaws. Recall is the share of real flaws the tool finds. F1 combines the two into one score between 0 and 1. The authors computed these per project and then took the plain average over the ten projects, which is called a macro average [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10].

### Data and setup
- The test set is 10 C# projects with 3–10 files each, 3,145–5,317 characters each, and 63 vulnerabilities in total [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6].
- The flaws come from six categories: SQL injection, cross-site scripting, hard-coded secrets, command injection, weak encryption and outdated libraries [@gnieciak2025large, p. 5].
- The paper says the projects were "prepared" with "a random number of vulnerabilities" [@gnieciak2025large, p. 5], but the abstract calls them "real-world" projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 1]. [I] The sizes suggest small purpose-built examples, not real software.
- Temperature (a setting that controls how random the LLM's answers are), model versions and actual run costs are not reported. List prices per million tokens are given [@gnieciak2025large, p. 5].
- The harness code is public [@gnieciak2025large, p. 1].

### Key findings
- [V] Mean F1: GPT-4.1 0.797, Mistral Large 0.753, DeepSeek V3 0.750, against Snyk Code 0.546, CodeQL 0.386 and SonarQube 0.260 [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10].
- [V] The gap comes mainly from recall. The LLMs reach mean recall 0.783–0.877, the SAST tools 0.187–0.523. Mean precision is closer: 0.723–0.783 for LLMs, 0.567–0.686 for SAST [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10].
- [I] Pooling the raw counts instead of averaging per project gives SAST precision of about 0.74–0.87 against 0.74–0.79 for the LLMs, and Snyk's F1 rises to about 0.70 (our arithmetic from the raw tables [@gnieciak2025large, p. 8]). The averaging method widens the gap.
- [V] LLMs were fast. CodeQL took 185.9–213.1 seconds per project and GPT-4.1 took 3.5–17.8 seconds [@gnieciak2025large, p. 9].
- [A] All LLMs named the right file but always gave the wrong line and column [@gnieciak2025large, p. 11].
- [V] LLMs invented findings. For example, GPT-4.1 flagged a current version of a library (Newtonsoft.Json 13.0.3) as outdated [@gnieciak2025large, p. 12].
- [A] The authors recommend LLMs for early, broad checks during development and SAST for high-assurance audits [@gnieciak2025large, p. 12].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [I] The benchmark is tiny: 63 flaws in projects small enough to fit easily in one prompt [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]. This suits LLMs and says little about real repositories.
- [V] Wrong line locations were not counted against the LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]. [I] SAST tools got no such leniency, so the comparison is tilted towards the LLMs.
- [V] When a tool reported nothing on a project, its precision was recorded as 0.000 and averaged in [@gnieciak2025large, p. 9]. [I] This lowers SAST precision.
- [I] Each model ran once, with no repeat runs, no statistical tests and no confidence intervals. LLM answers can vary between runs.
- [I] Default SAST settings were used, and "outdated libraries" is normally the job of a different tool type. Both may disadvantage the SAST tools.
- [I] There are no results per vulnerability type, and no actual cost, although prices are listed.

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- [A] The authors call for studying prompt design and building a hybrid in which classic tools and LLMs prioritise and verify findings [@gnieciak2025large, p. 11].
- [I] The lenient location rule for LLMs is one of the scoring differences behind gap G1 (no shared evaluation protocol across studies).
- [I] The study uses small, synthetic-looking projects in one language, so it does not touch gap G2 (a fair three-way test on real, recent code with repository context).
- [I] It lists prices but reports no cost per real flaw found, which is the subject of gap G6.

### Why it matters for your research
This is one of the few head-to-head tests of commercial-grade SAST against frontier LLMs, and the only one in our set on C#. It supports the claim that LLMs beat SAST on small, self-contained code. But it is weak evidence. Use it as one data point in the "LLMs win on small code" group, and always pair it with the larger real-code studies that point the other way. It is also a good teaching example of how a scoring choice, such as averaging per project, can change a headline result.

### Connections to other papers
- It is one side of contradiction C3 in the evidence matrix (LLM vs SAST rankings reverse between settings). CASTLE also finds LLMs ahead on small C programs [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]. CodeQL beats LLMs on accuracy on synthetic test suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- At repository scale, LLM tools flag up to 77.4% of functions (preprint) [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7], and most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 11].
- [I] The "LLMs find more but are noisier" pattern also appears in deininger2026open, where SAST tools are more precise than every LLM at a realistic vulnerability rate [@deininger2026open, p. 8].

> **Takeaway:** On CASTLE, a new set of 250 small hand-written C programs, the best LLMs (top score 977 for GPT-o3-Mini) beat all 13 static analysers and 2 formal verification tools (best 661). The programs are tiny and the result table has counting problems, so the win may not carry over to real code. The authors' own test on a 400-line program suggests it does not.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Richard A. Dubniczky, Krisztofer Zoltan Horvát, Tamás Bisztray, Mohamed Amine Ferrag, Lucas C. Cordeiro, Norbert Tihanyi |
| Year | 2025 |
| Venue | Lecture Notes in Computer Science (proceedings book chapter) |
| Status | Peer-reviewed (published chapter). Our copy is the arXiv version (2503.09433, v2), so numbers may differ from the published chapter. |
| Identifier | DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-98208-8_15 |
| Paper type | Benchmark dataset paper with a comparative evaluation |
| Relevance to us | High — RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5 |

### In plain words
A benchmark is a fixed test set that lets different tools be scored in the same way. This paper builds a new benchmark for the C language called CASTLE. It then runs three kinds of tools on it. The first kind is static analysers (SAST), which read code and apply rules. The second is formal verification (FV) tools, which try to prove mathematically that a program cannot reach a bad state. The third is LLMs, chatbot-style AI models asked to review the code.

Each program has at most one flaw, and each flaw is tied to a CWE. A CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) is a standard catalogue number for a type of weakness, for example CWE-476 for "null pointer dereference". On these short programs the large LLMs come out on top.

### How they did it
Security experts wrote the 250 programs by hand and marked the exact vulnerable line [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 6]. The authors ran 13 static analysers, 2 FV tools and 10 LLMs [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]. The LLMs were prompted zero-shot (no examples, no extra training) to act as a "professional security analyst". The prompt also told them the scoring rule: "5 points for each vulnerability you find, but get -1 for all false positives" [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9].

Results are given as true and false positives (correct and wrong warnings), precision, recall and accuracy. The authors also define a new metric, the CASTLE Score. It gives points for each correct find, a bonus for more dangerous CWEs, points for staying quiet on clean programs, and penalties for each false alarm [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 10]. The maximum is 1,250 [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 12].

### Data and setup
- 25 CWEs × 10 programs = 250 programs: 150 vulnerable and 100 clean. They are 7–164 lines long, with a mean of 42 [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 6].
- The CWEs come mostly from the MITRE Top-25 list of most dangerous weaknesses [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 7].
- Tool versions are reported, for example CodeQL 2.20.1 and ESBMC 7.8.1 [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]. LLM temperature, model snapshots and costs are not reported.
- The dataset and tool wrappers are public [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 1].

### Key findings
- [V] CASTLE Scores: GPT-o3-Mini 977, GPT-o1 962, DeepSeek R1 956, GPT-4o 954. The best non-LLM tools are ESBMC 661 and CodeQL 634 [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
- [V] Large LLMs have high recall: GPT-o3-Mini 78% with 63% precision, DeepSeek R1 90% with 47% precision. Small open models are weaker, for example Llama 3.1 8B with 20% precision [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
- [A] CodeQL is the best SAST tool and finds 29% of the flaws, against a SAST average of 23% [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 12]. [I] The paper writes this as "45/150", which is 30%; 29% matches a different denominator in the table (see Limitations).
- [V] Some SAST tools are swamped by noise. Splint raised 1,027 false alarms and CodeThreat 1,101, which gave them negative scores [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
- [V] Combining two non-LLM tools helps: ESBMC plus CodeQL scores 814, up from 661 for ESBMC alone [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 13]. No LLM-plus-tool combination was tested.
- [A] The authors say reasoning models "consistently produced fewer false positives" [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14]. [I] Their own table shows this only for OpenAI's o-series: DeepSeek R1 made 166 false alarms against 116 for GPT-4o [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
- [A] FV tools raise almost no false alarms but cannot detect issues such as SQL injection or hard-coded passwords [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 12].
- [A] In a preliminary test on one program of more than 400 lines, LLMs raised more false alarms and most missed the single hidden flaw. No numbers are given [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [I] Counting problem: there are 150 vulnerable programs, but true positives plus missed flaws add up to 154–179 for all 10 LLMs and 155–157 for four SAST tools [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]. Recall and accuracy therefore use unclear denominators. Quote exact numbers with this caveat.
- [V] LLMs returned the content of the flagged line so that small line-number errors could be corrected [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 8]. [I] No such help is described for the SAST tools, and the prompt reveals the scoring rule. Both favour the LLMs.
- [A] The programs are tiny and single-file. Real flaws often span many files [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14].
- [I] The CASTLE Score weights are the authors' own choice and are not checked against any outside standard.
- [I] There are no per-CWE results, no statistical tests, and no costs. The authors say repeated runs differ by under 3%, but do not say how many repeats there were [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14].
- [A] Because the tests are public, tool vendors could tune for them; the authors suggest refreshing the dataset [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14].

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- [A] The authors call for refreshing the tests and studying scale-up to large codebases [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14].
- [I] The prompt that reveals the scoring scheme and the new CASTLE Score both feed gap G1: studies use incompatible metrics and no shared protocol.
- [I] Single-file synthetic programs leave gap G2 open (a fair three-way test on real, recent code with repository context).
- [I] No hybrid LLM-plus-tool run is tested, and no cost is reported, so the paper says nothing on gap G4 (independent tests of hybrids) or gap G6 (cost per real flaw found).

### Why it matters for your research
CASTLE has the widest tool panel in our set: 13 SAST tools including commercial ones, 2 FV tools and 10 LLMs, all on one controlled benchmark with line-level labels. It is the cleanest evidence that frontier LLMs beat SAST on small, self-contained C code. For a comparative review it is just as useful as a contrast case. Its own large-file test, together with the real-code studies, shows why "who wins" depends on the size and realism of the code.

- It sits on the "LLMs win" side of contradiction C3, together with gnieciak2025large [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10]. On synthetic Java and C/C++ suites, CodeQL beats LLMs on accuracy [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At project scale, most tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 11].

- Its CodeQL recall of 29% supports agreement G4 (SAST recall is low outside synthetic suites), as do zhou2024comparison (preprint) [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6] and li2026llm [@li2026llm, p. 7].
